I wish to table a copy of a letter dated June 6, 1950, and attached memorandum addressed to me as Minister of Finance, and Hon. D. L. Campbell, premier of Manitoba, constituting a progress report of the joint commission on flood damage in Manitoba, which, as the house is aware, consists of Mr. J. B. Carswell, representing the dominion government, and Mr. D. Bruce Shaw, representing the government of Manitoba.
Perhaps I might add a few words. As the house is aware, I flew out to Manitoba on Tuesday afternoon. I had three purposes in mind. I was anxious to see a bit of the flood damage which had been caused. I wanted to discuss with the members of the commission and with the Manitoba government the progress which had been made in ascertaining the damage caused by the flood. I found that my visit was a most helpful one. The weather was such that I was able to fly down in the afternoon over the upper part of the valley. I found that the flood waters certainly had receded extremely rapidly, and it was quite clear that large areas which had previously been flooded were already clear and that seeding was taking place even in some of those areas. We flew at a low level. Some of the towns, particularly Morris, had suffered great physical damage to almost every building in the municipality.
The next morning I was taken to some sections of the city of Winnipeg, which I was informed had suffered the worst damage, and certain sections of St. Vital, and the Wildwood area. It is quite clear today; while it looked pretty bad, it was obvious that a week or ten days ago it must have looked a great deal worse.
In the evening I had an opportunity of discussing with members of the commission the draft of the report which in final form has been tabled today. Mr. Campbell, the premier of Manitoba, participated in those discussions. The following morning I had an opportunity of meeting the members of the Manitoba cabinet and, finally, in the afternoon, had a concluding meeting with the members of the commission and received their report in final form which I have tabled today.
I do not intend to discuss the details of the report. It speaks for itself. I just want to say that I do not think one can speak in too high terms of the way in which the people of Manitoba and of the city of Winnipeg have responded to the calls made upon them by this terrible disaster. I was greatly impressed

by the way in which individual citizens were setting to work to clean up their houses and to do repairs to their buildings. I had a chance to call at the offices of the Manitoba flood relief fund. They have done a magnificent job in raising funds voluntarily from all parts of Canada and abroad. The municipal government and the local government authorities seem to be working in harmony to co-ordinate the various services at the different levels of government. It struck me that the rehabilitation authorities, in the assistance they were giving to repair of the damage caused by this disaster, were operating very efficiently.
I reported of course to my colleagues yesterday, and placed before them this report. In the light of the facts disclosed in this report the government has decided to include in the supplementary estimates, which I hope will be tabled within the next week or ten days, an appropriation for $12,500,000 as an initial payment to the government of Manitoba to assist it in discharging the obligations which it will have to carry out as a result of the flood damage.
In addition, hon. members will see from the report that the committee has suggested that in the urban areas of Winnipeg certain, emergency diking measures might be developed in order to prevent a recurrence of these floods. As was the case in the Fraser valley, the dominion government of course would participate on the basis of 75-25 in the costs of such works, if it is decided to proceed with them; and in the supplementary estimates an appropriate amount will be included to cover an estimate of what might be required in that connection in the forthcoming period.

speechtext:
At eleven o'clock last night I was discussing the situation in our north country. I had asked the minister questions as to what was being done by Canada to train our native population in the north country to assist in our defences. I had pointed out that Russia, according to the reports we have received, was making great use of the Eskimos and other natives in northern Siberia and on the Aleutian islands, training them as scouts and patrols and for other work in that country. We also have reports that they have established many scientific stations in their north country, and that they are experimenting with the growing of crops and food1 so that the people of that area may be self-supporting. All this of course proves to us that Russia intends to keep that country in such a condition that if she should decide to attack she would be in a position to do so.
The reports also mention the necessity for the training of our soldiers in north country fighting, and contend that great attention should be paid to the defences of the Yukon and northern Canada.
It was very interesting after the Sweetbriar training exercise to read the United States papers. I may say that the United States is not only equally interested in the defence of the north country; I think she is probably more interested than we are, on account of Alaska, and also of the threat to themselves.
I should like to read from the Christian Science Monitor, the issue of March 16, which contains the opinion of that paper, and I think it also expresses the opinion of a good many people in the United States, as to the success of the Exercise Sweetbriar. The article is headed:	"Whitehorse tagged for


U.S. defence role". I may say that Whitehorse has been mentioned by the United States as the Gibraltar of the north. The article reads:
Divided Opinions
High Canadian and American military officials who attended as observers were inclined to be noncommittal when questioned openly about the success of Sweetbriar. OH the record, some expressed shock at the state of northern defences, while others optimistically believed that all will be well and that any deficiencies would be remedied as a result of the operation.
That neither the United States nor Canada is ready for Arctic warfare was made clear during the ten days in which a force of some 5,000 soldiers manoeuvred and fought with a so-called "aggressor" which had overrun Alaska and then threatened the whole continent.
I do not think that our department of defence, or the United States department of defence, believed that Sweetbriar would be a hundred per cent successful. By that I mean they did not believe that the equipment they had would be entirely suitable to the climate, nor did they believe that our soldiers were sufficiently trained in Arctic warfare. The success of Sweetbriar would probably be measured in the lessons that were learned, and also in a determination of the weaknesses of our northern defences. I am satisfied that our department learned many lessons, with regard to both the training of the men and the use of equipment in this barren and cold country.
I am sure we must all realize the great difficulties experienced in training men for warfare in a northern climate where there are deep snows, and where the temperature falls to sixty and sometimes seventy degrees below zero. I realize that it must be difficult for the equipment to stand up; I realize that it must be very difficult indeed for men to use the equipment. This test will be a great success if the defence department has learned the lessons of the difficulties in the north country and has tried to correct the difficulties and to prepare for the future.
I might suggest in this connection that one of the great problems that faces the Canadian army is training for these operations. Yesterday the leader of the opposition said that in connection with the training of our air force we have every facility in this broad country of ours for training airmen. We also have the facilities and territory for the training of our tank and other corps. For winter training also Canada is as well suited as any other country, especially Russia. I would impress upon the minister the necessity of more winter training; instead of having so much training of our men in the summer camps, our active forces and our militia should confine their training to a great extent to the wintertime. I do not imagine this would be a very

popular suggestion with the men in the armed forces, but looking toward the necessity of this type of training it seems to me we could and should devote more of our time to such training.
I should like to pay a tribute to our national research council. A few moments ago I said that our department must have found many weaknesses in the equipment used in the northern country. I have had the pleasure and the honour of being a member of the committee on national research. On several occasions I have had the opportunity of visiting the national research building, and I have seen for myself the work which is going on there. Without divulging any secrets- it is amusing to go through the national research council and be told that there are certain things which are very secret and that you must not tell anything about them- I am satisfied that not a single member of parliament who goes into the national research council could come out and divulge any of the secrets that he sees there. He does know, however, that in a general way great work is being done by the scientists of Canada for the development of some of these matters I mentioned that are related to our defence.
Another matter of great interest to the Canadian people is the dispersal of our munitions plants. This subject has been discussed before in the house on numerous occasions. There is no question that in a great country like Canada, with the possibilities of bombing in wartime, our munitions plants should not be centred in thickly populated areas. They should be scattered across the country. In the last war Russia was prepared to retire to the Ural mountains; she had behind those mountains munitions plants to supply her troops. We in Canada would make a great mistake if we concentrated the making of munitions in large centres which might be subjected to bombing.
I had intended to speak about civilian defence, but the matter has been discussed at some length already. From the minister's statement I would judge that we are following to a greater or lesser degree the plan being carried out in the United States. I am informed that over there state and federal officials are working together. For instance the minister said yesterday that it would take practically all the money allocated to our defence estimates to provide radar protection in this country. In the United States I understand that under their civilian defence measures they have made provision to train 150,000 aircraft spotters, to augment the seeing eye, or radar. I should judge that something like that is
Supply-National Defence planned for Canada. In the United States they also have training courses for the handling of radiation injuries, and they are issuing excellent booklets and other instructions in this connection. This of course is a great work, and if the same is being done in Canada I am sure satisfactory results will be obtained.
We have heard much about recruiting, and the debate has been interesting. However, as my leader pointed out yesterday, the mere fact of having a thousand names or five hundred names on a roll is not sufficient; it does not indicate to the house or the people in Canada the extent of the training. The number of men who are taken into camp would show what our training is, and would reflect the usefulness of our reserve and other units.
In the matter of recruiting I would say that we must have good feeling throughout the country before our efforts can be successful. The people must be sympathetic toward the armed services. They have not been getting all the information they would like, nor have we in the House of Commons. If recruiting is to be successful, the people must feel sympathetically toward the navy, the army and the air force.
There have been some developments recently which have not tended to increase the confidence of our people in our armed forces. One of these had to do with the marking of graves overseas. I was pleased to hear the minister say yesterday that this defect had been corrected, a result, I am sure, of the widespread criticism across the country that a great mistake had been made. That mistake is being corrected, I imagine at considerable expense.
There is also the matter of medals. This may not be strictly a defence matter, but it is connected with the army. There was and is today widespread resentment across Canada that the medals given to the soldiers who fought in the last war are not inscribed with the names and numbers of those soldiers, as was done after the first war. These may seem small matters, but they do arouse resentment and dissatisfaction.
A short time ago there was an announcement with respect to a change in the tunes and airs used in the navy. I am not well qualified to discuss this matter, but I do know that in many sections of Canada there is resentment over this change. The people who resent it most are those whose sons were the first to enlist in the last two wars, and who would be the first to enlist in the navy today should necessity arise. I refer particularly to the replacing of "Rule Britannia" by "O Canada". These conditions do not help in

Supply-National Defence recruiting, and the government and the department before making such hasty changes should give careful consideration to them.
Perhaps we did not need to pay much attention to it, but I did listen to the hon. member for Ontario last night defend the defence department and criticize all those who had criticized that department. I could not help remembering that that great defender of the faith, the hon. member for Ontario, was the man who suggested that the description "Royal" should be taken away from the Royal Canadian Navy and the Royal Canadian Air Force. However, as I said before, no one is taking seriously what he said. The government, I hope, does not take it seriously, and I am sure the same feeling prevails throughout the country. Such a change would give rise to so much resentment that it would have grave repercussions.
In closing I should like to make reference to two units in my own province. My own town of Sussex is the headquarters of the Princess Louise Hussars. We are very proud of this unit, of which the hon. member for Westmorland is second in command. I have been informed by the defence department that it is one of the best, if not the best trained militia unit in Canada. We also take pride in our Canadian Scottish regiment. It, too, is well trained. There is a feeling in the maritime provinces that we should have down there a permanent force unit, and I would ask the minister if he is giving consideration to the appointment of the Princess Louise Hussars as a permanent force unit, and if not whether he will do so.

subtopic: QUESTION AS TO PROCLAMATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Royal has mentioned one or two points about which I should like to make some comment. He asked first whether we are training Eskimos and Indians in the far north. We are not endeavouring to give them military training, because in the nature of their living conditions they are fully occupied with survival. However, they are working very closely indeed with the armed forces in the north, and have been used extensively in transportation, construction, and the like. We have also borrowed to a great extent-from their knowledge of northern living conditions, the first thing that forces operating in the north must learn.
The hon. member suggested that we should emphasize winter training. I can assure him that that is being done more and more. At Wainwright, Shilo, Rivers, Churchill, Val-cartier and other places, both active and reserve force units are receiving winter training. To as large an extent as possible that is being supplemented by local training in week-end exercises carried out by units right


across Canada. More of that is being done than ever before, and certainly the experience of Exercise Sweetbriar was that only personnel who were highly trained in winter warfare can hope to operate efficiently in extremely cold weather.
I appreciate what the hon. gentleman said about the Princess Louise Hussars, which he said was one of the best units in Canada. I do not think it is desirable to contemplate making a reserve unit, which is carrying on so well, into a permanent force unit. I am sure the hon. member who is second in command would have something to say about that.
With regard to the remarks of the leader of the opposition last night, there are one or two corrections I should like to make. With regard to artillery practice, the hon. gentleman said that there was no firing practice, and he made reference to competitive firing. There are unit exercises; the units do go to camp as batteries, and there is competitive firing. The hon. gentleman is quite right in the impression he gathered that the Royal Canadian Artillery Association has not yet put up a cup for competitive battery firing. Reading the remarks of the hon. gentleman together, he is quite right, but there are unit exercises and competitive firing being carried on. We are putting emphasis less and less on battery competition and more and more on the work of the teams; but still competition is desirable, and I understand that battery competitions will be reinstituted this year.
The hon. gentleman referred to the remarks of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and on page 3396 of Hansard he is shown as having quoted the remarks of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. But those remarks should be supplemented by what the Secretary of State for External Affairs went on to say:
We do not yet know how It will affect the detailed responsibilities of any particular member of the alliance.
You will see that the Secretary of State for External Affairs is referring not only to the position of Canada but to the position of the other eleven countries in the alliance. It is still too early to say how this principle of balanced forces will work. The minister went on to say:
As far as this government is concerned, in our defence policy we have already accepted this principle and have been trying to relate our policy to the defence of an area rather than merely to the defence of a country. We have been going on that principle and we will gladly do what we can to continue its application.
That was a point I made yesterday, and of course that is perfectly clear.

As reported on page 3396 of Hansard the leader of the opposition regretted, and I quote:
-we are not to be informed of any changes that are to be made in the organization of our defence forces in keeping with this ailocation of special tasks.
I cannot inform him of any changes, because no changes have yet been made, either here or in other countries. The principle has just been agreed to. What I say would equally be said by any of the defence ministers of any other country.
I quote further the remarks of the leader of the opposition as reported on page 3399:
I do earnestly hope that the minister will indicate there is some intention of examining our present structure so that there can be a reallocation of forces in keeping with the statement of the minister of external affairs only three days ago.
Our program and the progress we are making in connection with it is under constant review. That has been indicated before. Changes are made in the program as they may be considered necessary. Now that this principle has been agreed to, we shall of course co-operate loyally and frankly and completely with the other north Atlantic countries in causing the allocation of our forces, their nature and composition and equipment, to be examined, and we will accept for consideration the views of the other countries. There is no doubt about that. When I said yesterday that this principle would not cause any immediate change, by "immediate" I had in mind a change within the period covered by these estimates, namely, 1950-51. In the future it may result in change, or in many changes. It certainly will result in some, both in this country and in others. But in view of the nature of our role and of the forces we have, those changes are not likely to be of a drastic nature materially affecting anything that has been done in the past in the way of defence.
As I say, we have never considered our defence as a thing that is separate, as something to be undertaken by us separately; we have always considered it as part of total defence in a total war.
Just a further word in this connection. It must be evident to hon. members that the reason why we went into the North Atlantic treaty-indeed, we are one of the nations which first suggested it and strongly supported it-is that we felt it to be in our vital interest and in the vital interest of the freedom of all nations that this treaty should be formulated and supported. We mean to carry out to the full everything that is involved in our participation in that treaty, and from what we have seen we have every reason to believe
9, 1950	3411
Supply-National Defence that that is the view of the other eleven nations who are participating in it. We went into the treaty because of our national interest, and we will support the treaty because we have entered into it and because it is in our national interest to do so.
It was emphasized by the hon. member for Cape Breton South that this is a treaty for the defence of peace. Of course it is. That aim is out in the forefront of the desirable objectives to be attained by this means. I indicated before that the North Atlantic treaty organization has as its objectives to deter aggression, and if necessary to defend ourselves against aggression and to defeat the aggressor. It has been said repeatedly by other leaders in the North Atlantic treaty countries that they believe that this is possible. Did we not believe it to be possible, the future would indeed look dark. But it is our conviction that by working together along the lines that have been indicated we can achieve these results.
With regard to some of the specific questions asked by the leader of the opposition, there is certain information that is not available yet but I shall deal with some of the questions now.
The hon. gentleman said that he would like to have information as to the number of units in the active and reserve forces of the army, navy and air force, divided into the differennt types of units. As he must appreciate, there must be several hundred units in the active forces and well on to a thousand units in the reserve, with divisions into different types of units.
Then he asked for details of the equipment which they should have and what they actually have. There are two schedules of equipment, one for training equipment and the other for mobilization equipment. With regard to training equipment, I can tell him that all the reserve units have all the equipment they need. There are large reserves and pools of equipment for reserve unit training at the different commands across the country. If any unit can use additional equipment, it only needs to ask the local G.O.C. and the equipment will be made available. There is no shortage of reserve army equipment.
With regard to war equipment or mobilization stores, information as to this is contained in army form G1098. There is an equipment table for each type of unit in the armed forces. There are 400 different volumes like these, each one of them about the size of a small Eaton's catalogue, and of course they are secret. I do not know anything that the enemy would like to obtain more than the strength of trained personnel in each type of unit, so as to show our whole battle order, its effectiveness, and the establishment figures

Supply-National Defence for mobilization. There is a further reason why this is regarded as confidential, namely, that it would disclose information not only about our own establishment but also about the establishments of countries with which we are allied.
On the question of security I should add that often we would very much like to give information but we cannot do so because it is shared with other countries. There is also the fact that one of the things a prospective aggressor would like to find out is how accurate his own sources of information are, in order that he can check his own espionage and information services. Even though intrinsically the information may not be of great importance to a prospective aggressor, it is of great value in enabling him to verify the accuracy of his sources of information in respect of other matters.
I can give a figure as to equipment. Some time ago I asked for a statement showing the quantity of equipment it was estimated we would need during the first year of an emergency should it arise. For the army it totalled 171,381,981 different pieces of equipment. At that time we had in stores 119,336,386, which in numbers represents about two-thirds of the equipment needed for the first year of a war should it arise. I think that will give the hon. member substantially what he wants, in the way in which it can be made available.
The hon. member asked for the expenditure to be devoted to each branch of the services during the present year. As hon. members know, it is not the practice in this or in other countries to keep books by units. Equipment is not dealt with in dollar value per unit. It is dealt with on a physical issue basis. Army units are not accounting units in the sense of keeping books showing all costs in terms of dollars. Estimates in Canada, the United States and the United Kingdom are not built up on a unit basis. To provide the hon. member with the information he wants would require the complete reconstruction of our accounting practice, and a complete review of every individual item that was issued or went to any unit. So that the information is simply not available.
The hon. member asked for similar figures with regard to headquarters, and the amount that is being asked for the maintenance thereof. The same answer applies. I have, however, obtained information which may be interesting particularly in view of the question put by the hon. member for Calgary East. He asked what progress was being made in reducing the proportion of the numbers in headquarters staffs to other units in


the armed forces. As at the 31st December, 1949, 9-1 per cent of the armed forces were in headquarters staff, and at other units 90-9 per cent. As at the 31st March, 1950, 8-7 per cent were at headquarters of all kinds and 91-3 per cent were with units, representing a trend in a desirable direction. In view of the nature of modern defence forces and the necessity for maintaining administrative and planning staffs to deal with very much larger forces should the need arise, I think the figures I have mentioned are not out of line. We will continue, however, to endeavour to put more and more personnel into operational units. Of course that is a very desirable objective.
In this connection I might mention two facts with regard to the navy, which will be of interest. I was asked to what degree the navy could be made fully operational in a short time. I think I can say to an exceedingly good degree at the present time, and that all ships in commission can be fully operational within a matter of hours rather than days. At the present time 41-5 per cent of the personnel of the navy are on commissioned ships, representing a very large proportion, much larger than any other navies with which we are familiar, and at least as much as we would want them to be.
We have made a similar comparison as to the air force, and we find that on the basis of man hours of flying per month the Royal Canadian Air Force compares favourably with other comparable air forces. At this stage of its development that seems to us to be as good a test as any.
I should say something as to a matter about which there has been some comment in the press resulting from the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I refer to the future role of the infantry. At page 3189 of Hansard for June 5 the Secretary of State for External Affairs had this to say:
This principle may come to mean . . .
Then I will omit certain words.
. . . and eventually, possibly, to the abandonment of the old concept of defence by great masses of conscripted infantry, the bulk of which would be reservists called up on the outbreak of war.
I have not had an opportunity to discuss this point with my colleague, because he has been away since I saw the statement. I have no doubt, however, from the language used, and from our common knowledge of the situation, that he has in mind possible developments, particularly on the continent of Europe, which might bring about that result. With the increased application of scientific techniques and increased1 mechanization, there would not be the same value in great masses of conscripted infantry, but I

should like to make it very plain that we in Canada do not envisage any considerable change in the role of infantry in the foreseeable future. I think it would be a great mistake for any such misconception to go out, because it might adversely affect people interested in the infantry, and recruiting for infantry reserve units. At the end of the second world war I believe experience showed that the infantry were just as important as they had ever been in the history of modern warfare, and probably more so. I believe that the trend of modern development in the immediate future will increase the importance of infantry, because there are developments coming in weapons and projectiles which will increase the defensive power of infantry against armour. So that while the concept of great masses of infantry may cease to be so prevalent, that does not reduce in any way whatever the great importance of the infantry soldier with his modern weapons-sixteen of them-in modern warfare. If he is fully trained and equipped with those weapons, then he may become the determining factor in the final stage of any such warfare.
Do not let what I have just said, however, in an endeavour to correct what may be a misapprehension, lead anyone to think I underestimate the importance of the other arms of the service or of the other services. They all have their roles, and they must all work together as a team. I must agree completely with the remarks of the leader of the opposition and others with regard to the role of the air force. Those remarks are completely in accord with the policy we have had. Certainly from the point of view of immediate activity in the event of an emergency, in a war as far away as we hope the centre of activities would be, the air force will play a big role. On that account we are putting the emphasis we are on the air force, as regards both organizing squadrons and equipment. At the same time it is much too early to say that that role can be played to the complete exclusion of anything else. As I say, defence is a team operation, and while we mean to support the idea of balanced collective forces between nations, the time when that is likely to produce major changes in the allocation of forces within Canada is not yet upon us. The matter is just receiving consideration at the international level, and while there will be changes in the foreseeable future which I shall be glad to discuss when they arise, they will be changes in the development of forces and the standardization of equipment, which will provide the partnership of the north Atlantic nations
Supply-National Defence with the power which is essential to the preservation of peace, or, if peace cannot be secured, the restoration of peace.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to deal immediately with one or two points that have been made by the Minister of National Defence because it seems to me they go to the root of the understanding of this problem with which we are dealing, the most important single departmental problem the government faces.
Referring to the discussion which took place last night about the competitive firing practice at artillery camps, the minister indicated that he has checked on the situation since then and has found that the view I expressed was substantially correct. But what disturbs me is that the answer he has now given is not correct. He states that there are exercises as units, and he says that there is competitive firing as units. Mr. Chairman, I say most emphatically that is not so.
The present plans call for no competitive firing by artillery units at Petawawa or the other artillery camp this year; nor do they have the opportunity for movement and training as units, which in itself is the basis of training for active service. I can only point this out, because unless we understand these things we do not understand what the state of training actually is, and what is being produced by the money that is being spent. As the minister has already indicated, the competitive firing that is done by the artillery is under competitions that are arranged by .the Canadian Artillery Association. None of that firing practice will be carried out this summer, unless there is a change between now and then, which seems unlikely, in view of the fact that the units will be starting to move into camp almost any day, and will continue to progressively move into camp at different times during the summer.
The procedure that is followed is that the artillery units send men from their own units. Those men are brought into training groups, and receive excellent training in special subjects. They do participate in firing; they do see the theory of firing explained and carried out in actual firing practice, but they do not operate as firing units. Artillery that does not operate as a firing unit is a long distance from being even near the point of readiness to prepare for active service conditions. That is true also of the infantry. At the infantry camp the infantry do not train as field units under field conditions. There again the members of those units are given excellent training in the details of infantry work. As a result of that training
3414	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence they will be able to go back and pass on that training to others with whom they will be associated in the training at the local armouries and elsewhere. There again, excellent though the training may be, the units are not getting that type of field training as units, with the use of their own fire power, in competitive contests. Such training is the basic qualification for obtaining real results.
As I believe the minister must know, the Canadian Artillery Association has indicated it intends to discuss this subject at its meeting in the last week of October, but that is for next year, not this year. So it is with the infantry. They are discussing this subject. Everyone recognizes the difficulties, but, in the name of common sense and in the name of preparation for real defence, let us not accept any explanation that is not in keeping with reality. If the minister was informed in accordance with the statement he made to the house this morning, I suggest that he ascertain exactly what training the artillery units will be receiving at Petawawa, Shilo and other artillery camps across the country, as well as what training the infantry will receive in the field, as units, under unit competitive circumstances.
Referring to the assumption of our obligations, the minister said that we mean !to carry out to the full everything that is involved in that treaty. I believe those are his exact words, or so close to them I feel he will accept them as a correct statement of the effect of the words he used. If the minister means just what he says, that we mean to carry out everything that is involved, then of course he means that it' is agreed this government will carry out what was described by the minister of external affairs as the new principle recognized by this recent London meeting. That principle is that if one nation can perform a particular task, then those nations which cannot do it so well will leave that task to be done by that particular nation. The minister of external affairs qualified that, in what was much the most important part of his statement, by saying that this principle carried with it the necessity of knowing that the nation which had that special type of equipment would use it. That of course must be obvious; because if one nation is to let another nation concentrate on fast land armoured forces and does not provide them themselves, they will then place themselves in a position of pitiful weakness and utter helplessness, unless their failure to supply those forces was compensated by the existence of forces immediately available and in a state of war readiness the moment the call came-not war readiness three months from now, or six months from now, but war readiness today.


One fact that should be in the mind of every member of this committee is that when we are discussing the figures before us now we are not in a position of war readiness with regard' to any part of those forces in any number that could be recognized as substantial fulfilment of the agreement that was entered into in London. We are not within six months, at a minimum, of being able to carry out our part. That fact applies not only to the fulfilment of our part in any joint enterprise overseas, but also to the fulfilment of our part within our own country to meet the type of force that we would be called upon to meet if that force were brought to our shores by air or by sea; but presumably the threat would be by air.
In discussing these matters let us not regard the statement of what the realities are as a challenge either to the quality of the forces we possess or the earnestness of the effort that they are making. We have in our forces men and women doing their utmost to bring those forces to the highest level of training efficiency possible. One of the tragic stories of the democracies in a considerable part of this century is the lulling of the people by the assurances that they are ready when that term "readiness" is taken to mean readiness by our standards, not by the standards of readiness of the enemy we are called upon to face. Do not let anyone today forget the reassuring statements that were made before this last war; and do not let anyone forget the knowledge of everyone who participated as to the time it actually took to bring our training to the state that we were assured it possessed in the months and years before this last war.
As the Secretary of State for External Affairs has pointed out, this situation calls for immediate action. We cannot hope to have time to build up behind the ramparts of the sacrifice of other people. We must be prepared to take our part the moment these forces are needed. It will be the knowledge that we can do that and that other nations can do it that will be the one assurance we can ever have of peace.
As to the question of the changes envisaged by the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, there was a statement carried by Canadian Press and extensively published throughout Canada, on June 6, the day after the Secretary of State for External Affairs made his statement. I think that the first four paragraphs of that reported statement are of value-and I am quoting in this case from the Montreal Gazette-because they indicate statements that were made here to the Canadian Press. When the Canadian Press says that officers of the Department of National Defence made those statements, I

accept their word for it-and I feel sure that the minister will accept their word for it- that such statements were made. I quote from this report as follows:
Atlantic pact arms developments in the next few years hold a strong possibility of working big changes in Canada's forces and in plans to send overseas a third expeditionary force mainly composed of infantry in any new war, informed quarters said today.
Within five years, they said, the use of massed infantry could easily be obsolete. Such military efforts as the tight, tough land battles in Italy and the D-day landings in Normandy would be ruled out by the violence of mass destruction weapons.
This trend is of obvious and vital importance in view of Russia's stress on land forces, her almost unlimited ability to reinforce them and her relative immaturity in the scientific and technical fields.
Then may I emphasize these words which I am now quoting, still from that Canadian Press report:
Defence officials here said scientific advances now are moving towards push-button warfare at a pace which has defence headquarters constantly examining plans and revamping them.
That is a statement by the Canadian Press, based, according to that report, upon the statements of officials of the Department of National Defence. When I spoke last night of the concern that must be felt that we have no statement as to what the new plans are in relation to the situation envisaged by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in his statement last Monday, I referred to this very word "revamping". What I had hoped to hear, and what I think many other hon. members had hoped to hear, was a report on what revamping will be done and what rationalization will be done in accordance with the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, to the effect that each nation is going to perform, as part of this great team of free nations, the military task which it can best perform. His statement, if it was not specific in that regard, implied that the masses of infantry would be found amongst the teeming millions on the European continent which are being armed by the United States so largely today; and that we at a greater distance would And and train the harder hitting, more compact, mobile fighting forces in the air and on the land which could be quickly transported to any threatened area. In the light of that statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in the light of the situation disclosed, and in fact in the light of the difficulty that the minister has in dealing with individual problems, even with officials of the department in front of him-as indicated by the explanation given in regard to artillery training-I think we should' have the details before us.

The Minister of National Defence says that his books contain the records of a thousand infantry units. Certainly they do. But that fact presents no difficulty. There is no difficulty in putting down in a statement that there are so many infantry units, divided into active and reserve, and that there are so many artillery units. That just takes one line. Then there is no difficulty in putting down whether there are one hundred or two hundred, or whatever the number may be, active and reserve; and under each of these, the personnel of establishment and the personnel actually training; then under other headings, the units of the air force, active and reserve; machines in their possession; machines called for by establishment. The same with the navy; the number of ships, the number of units active, the number of units reserve, and the equipment they have-that would not take any volumes of books as was suggested by the minister. It is the kind of information that is available with regard to other departments of infinitely less importance than this one.
Even with what he said today, I still hope that the minister will agree to prepare a statement showing in simple and graphic form, first of all, the division of our defence areas into five commands, the inclusion under those commands of the armoured units, the ordinary infantry divisions, and the component units of those divisions, and the allocation of men to those units, so that we may have in front of us, in simple, graphic and understandable form, exactly what it is we are dealing with. Then, to take the case of the active units, of what use is it to us to be told that there are 40,000 men, or whatever the number may be? What we need to know is how many of these are in headquarters, how many at command headquarters, how many in permanent tasks that are not part of the active force, how many in the active force ready to go into service if they are called upon to do that. The relationship between the number at headquarters here, at command headquarters, at the various points throughout the country where there are detachments of this kind in relation to the number actively training, will give us the kind of picture we need.
In dealing with these remarks at this point, and in dealing with what the minister said about the state of training of the artillery, I simply have risen, first, to point out to him again the information that I have received from what I am satisfied is an entirely reliable source in regard to this; and second, to urge him once again to give us information which involves no measure of secrecy, but will

Supply-National Defence make clear to us the structure that we want to understand when we are putting up this money.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make plain the position as to artillery training. It is as stated by the leader of the opposition, and I do not think that what I said at the outset was any different, except that he, having been the former president of the Canadian Artillery Association, attaches very great importance to battery competitive practice. No doubt his own battery and regiment won the competition. I think that is so. However, emphasis is not placed by my advisers on that type of training at the present time. The note on this which I got since I came into the house is I believe substantially correct, and is in accordance with what both the leader of the opposition and myself said. Reserve force artillery units go to camp as units. Training is conducted there either on a course basis or on a unit battery basis. Battery training is now on the increase, and it is expected that several units will be trained that way this summer. Royal Canadian Artillery Association has not yet reinstated the pre-war competitions, but is considering a similar program to be instituted shortly. Initially competitive shoots are likely to be on a troop basis.
The oral information I had when I came into the house was that it had been decided to institute competitive shoots this summer. Apparently it is still being considered. It is a matter outside the control of the department; it is within the control of the association. I think what the leader of the opposition said and what I said are substantially in accord and in accordance with the facts.
With regard to the assurance of readiness, we have been very careful, and I think accurate, in giving any assurances. Admitting that everything the leader of the opposition said is true, and a great deal of it is, then that is every reason for our pressing on with training and equipment with a view to making the active force as militarily operational as it is possible for it to be, and for the reserve forces to approach just as rapidly as possible the standards we want to have for the active force.

speechtext:
There are one or two thoughts I should like to place before the minister and the committee this morning. But before doing so may I say that I realize the difficulties of the minister's position and of his department. Probably no one in the house would have thought it possible two or three years ago that within less than five years of the end of the fighting Canada would be faced with the necessity of appropriating at least half a billion dollars in any one year for defence purposes. That necessity of course arises

because of the unfortunate trend world affairs have taken, a trend which has resulted in the world being divided into two blocs, the peoples of each bloc worrying about war and discussing appropriations for defence in their respective legislative chambers. It is a very sad situation, but of course it is a situation that Canadians must face.
I do not think it will be questioned that if there should be another war it will be fought on a world-wide basis, though primarily in the northern hemisphere; and that the two chief participants will be the United States and Russia. These are facts which are perfectly obvious to everyone.
I believe that because of the North Atlantic treaty, and the steps that are being taken under that treaty, Canadians do not have to worry as much as they formerly did about warfare in the north Atlantic area. I am hopeful that that is the situation. While it may take some time, there is little doubt that eventually the nations which have signed that treaty and set up the North Atlantic council will be able to build up exceedingly strong defence forces which it would be very risky for Russia to attack.
However, as a member representing a constituency on the west coast I am very much disturbed by the attitude of the Minister of National Defence with regard to the Pacific. Just a few minutes ago he referred to Canada as a country as far away from the centre of activity as we hope we will be in the event of another war. I hope he is right, but I think that statement was absolutely unrealistic in view of the situation around the shores of the Pacific ocean.
In dealing with the defence for Canada on the Pacific coast yesterday, the minister used these words, as found at page 3380 of Hansard:
It is obvious that we are in the fortunate position of being well to the east of lines of defence which include Japan and the islands to the south and the Hawaiian islands, and Alaska in the north. We are not in the same exposed position in the Pacific as we are in the Atlantic.
Once again I fervently hope that he is right, but I believe that statements of that kind by the Minister of National Defence of Canada are very unfortunate because they will have the effect of lulling the Canadian people into a false sense of security with regard to the position on the Pacific. Statements of this kind are unfair to the Canadian people. I know the minister did not intend to be unfair. I think his intentions were perfectly good, but, in the final analysis, statements of that kind are unfair unless there is absolutely no doubt about their accuracy. Personally I believe that never in her whole history has Canada been in as

dangerous a position as she is today in the event of war. We are vulnerable on the Atlantic; we are vulnerable across the Arctic, and we are vulnerable on the Pacific.
As I said a moment ago, the two nations most directly involved in a third world war would be Russia and the United States. It is only reasonable to expect that one of these nations, sooner or later, in order to win will have to get at the other one. Russia's main objective in any such war would be to get at the United States. She could not possibly win a third world war without attacking the United States; and whether she attacks across the north Atlantic, across the Arctic or across the north Pacific, she must cross Canadian territory. That means, just as surely as night follows day, that in the event of a third world war Canada will be in the position of Belgium in the first one.
It is the duty of the members of the House of Commons to make it perfectly clear to the Canadian people that this is so, in order that there can be no misunderstanding of what Canada's position will be. The minister has said that we are safe behind the United States line in Alaska. Well, on April 1, General Dwight Eisenhower, the famous American leader, had this to say with regard to Alaska:
Strengthening Alaska and its major airfields against surprise airborne attack, by a permanent force of well-trained and equipped ground troops and a radar screen to detect and warn against air forays.
He stated that as one of the three main defence programs that should be undertaken by the United States. Two weeks later, General Omar N. Bradley, chairman of the United States joint chiefs of staff said he believed that Alaska is the weakest link in the United States military defence. The article goes on to say:
He added Alaska air bases must not fall into enemy hands since they could be used as long range bomber bases for attacks against the U.S.
Earlier, on February 22, we find this heading from San Francisco:	"U.S. sets up air
defences on west coast". The article goes on to say:
Establishment of a civil air raid warning system for U.S. western states was announced Tuesday.
The system is expected to be in operation within weeks. It will extend east to the rockies.
Special telephone communications will be set up within the entire western area. Civilian centres will be warned in less than a minute should the defence centre receive word that air attack is imminent.
Modern weapons and long-range aircraft were cited as a reason for the warning system.
And then a dispatch from Los Gatos, California, dated April 7, states:
Atomic-powered submarines may lead [DOT] attacks which would turn U.S. coastal cities into world war

Admiral Lockwood, retired wartime commander of the Pacific submarine fleet, warned that Russia "probably" has entered into a race with the U.S. to build the first "A-sub."
Admiral Lockwood predicted atomic-powered submarines would be "miracle warships" with an almost "unlimited" surface cruising range and capable of carrying atomic guided-missiles to U.S. shores completely undetected.
He pointed out that even the conventionally-powered Russian subs "can make a round-trip to the west coast, deliver guided missiles and return without refuelling."
This means of course that Russian submarines could stand off the Canadian coast and use guided missiles against our west coast Canadian cities, just as easily as they could against the American cities. These are some of the very serious possibilities we must face.
I have a statement from our own naval chief of staff, Vice Admiral Harold T. W. Grant. It was made in Victoria on April 28 of this year, and is reported in this way:
He reviewed the west coast defence picture and said it is becoming more important in view of the cold war and conditions in China. However, there were no plans to augment the Esquimalt-based fleet with ships from the east coast.
Then of course we had Exercise Sweetbriar, in the Yukon Territory and Alaska, which was based on the hypothesis that the Russians had taken Alaska. The exercise was to work out methods of stopping them in the vicinity of Whitehorse.
Yet I am afraid the situation is that Canadians, from the Minister of National Defence down, are still European-minded- or perhaps I should say Atlanticmninded. There is good reason why that should be our outlook as a people. We stem from European stock, and the first world war was essentially a European war. The last one was primarily European. Our thinking in regard to war naturally turns to the Atlantic and to Europe.
I remember so clearly the difficulty we had in the early months of 1942 in convincing the government that there was real danger on the Pacific coast. That was several months after the Japanese had struck at Pearl Harbor. On the coast we had practically no defences. It turned out later that we did not have as many aircraft on that coast as would have been carried by one Japanese aircraft carrier, and many of the aircraft we did have were very much out of date.
The Vancouver Sun took an active part in demanding that some steps be taken to defend the Pacific coast. Indeed, they took such an active part that they were dragged into police court by the defence department and fined because of some of the articles they had published. Members of the House of
3418	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence Commons from British Columbia also took a determined stand and went after the then minister of national defence pretty hard. At that time it was Hon. J. L. Ralston, who, incidentally, was one of Canada's greatest sons.
Those of us from British Columbia were much concerned about the situation. Our families and our people were out there, exposed to attack. The Americans had suffered at Pearl Harbor, and we knew there was no way of stopping the Japanese if they chose to invade the west coast. A day or two after I had attacked the defence department with considerable bitterness, the late Colonel Ralston called me out of the chamber, took me into room 16, and, in his friendly way, said, "Green, you are very much worried about the west coast. I can see that now. What is the trouble?" I tried to tell him, giving him my point of view. He said: "Well, you may be right; and if I could get one of my staff to agree with you I could do something about it. I'll tell you what we will do; we will go down and have a talk with the chief of staff. You can put up your side and he can put up his. I Shall just sit and listen; and we shall see what happens." Next day Colonel Ralston took me down to defence headquarters, where the late Lieutenant General Kenneth Stuart and I had a debate on the need for defending the Pacific coast. By the way, General Stuart was another great Canadian whose services to his country have never been fully appreciated. He gave his life for his country, just as did Colonel Ralston.
I think it would be most fitting that there should be placed in the halls of this building a statue of Colonel Ralston. He was a great battalion commander in the first war, commanding the 85th Nova Scotia Highlanders. His men loved him, and would follow him anywhere. During the second great war he served in a much less spectacular way by working here fifteen, eighteen and twenty hours a day doing a wonderful job. There is no doubt in my mind that his work during the second world war brought about his untimely death. I know of no Canadian more worthy of having a statue in his memory placed in the halls of this building than the late J. L. Ralston.
It was not long before the Japs took Kiska and to the south had a fleet on the way to invade either the Hawaiian islands or the west coast. Fortunately that fleet was defeated in the battle of Midway by the United States fleet air forces. Had it not been for that defeat, the west coast of Canada and the United States might well have been invaded. After taking Kiska the Japanese


started out to take Dutch Harbor, the next great United States base in Alaska. Fortunately they were turned back because the United States flyers flew out behind them and came in from the west, deceiving them into thinking there was a United States force behind them, and the Japanese turned back.
Canada then was inclined to be European-minded, and I am afraid that is still the situation. It would not be so bad if we were not so vulnerable on the north Pacific. Russia is a much tougher opponent in the Pacific than Japan ever could be, because Russia has Siberia. For years she has had a Siberian army able to carry on as an independent fighting force. That was the position in the recent war. The Russian Siberian forces were able to carry on, even though the European forces had been defeated.
Siberia reaches to within a few miles of Alaska. Russian airmen by the hundreds flew the route to Edmonton in order to take United States planes back to Siberia during the war. The Russians are accustomed to warfare in northern climates. There has been some discussion in this debate about the need of Canadians having training in Arctic fighting, and I think the defence department is realistic about that need. However, the Russians have been carrying on that type of training for years and are accustomed to fighting in cold weather. Added to Russia we now have China, with over 400 million people, the biggest reserve of manpower in the world today, and under the domination of Russia.
That is the situation we find in the Pacific area. Just the other day there was a dispatch in the Vancouver Sun dated May 31, just nine days ago. It is entitled, "Expansion in Asia Russia's main goal" and is from Warsaw by Daniel De Luce, Associated Press correspondent. The articles reads:
Some Poles within earshot of Moscow assert that this is the Russian planning for the next decade:
1.	Defensive consolidation in eastern Europe.
2.	Dynamic expansion of influence in Asia.
And again:
They say the Russians have more to fear than the western powers from a shooting scrape in Europe. It is Asia that's a soft touch, not the Rhine-with others to do the fighting, not the Soviet army.
They make this comparison of power:
American guns face Soviet frontiers in Germany and Austria. But where are they on the Asia mainland?
A hard-boiled communist is his own boss in Yugoslavia. Where is another like him in the Far East?
Marshall plan dollars continue to pour into western Europe, stronger industrially than ever in history. Where is the effective help for a weak Saigon or Bangkok or Rangoon?

The following is the substance of what I heard in Poland on a visa granted by the foreign ministry to encourage interest in a trade fair:
"You westerners don't see further than the end of your nose. You seem oblivious to the inner stresses and strains in our eastern bloc. You underestimate your strength in Europe. You are purblind to your weaknesses in Asia. Russia is winning there without having to fire a shot."
I have some suggestions to make to the minister with regard to the north Pacific. We should have there an air force ready to fight, with airfields adequately defended. There should be a coastal patrol able to deal with submarines. So far as I know there has never been any emphasis placed on Canada developing an air coastal patrol of that kind. It is essential for the defence of the cities, in fact for the defence of the whole west coast of Canada.
With regard to the army, I suggest that the permanent armoured brigade should be kept up to fighting strength and ready to strike at a moment's notice. That was the promise made to us in 1945 by the then minister of national defence; and I quote from page 1131 of Hansard of October 16, 1945, where the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is reported as having said:
This formation will be maintained as a trained field force, fully equipped, ready to meet whatever commitments may arise.
Such a force is essential for the defence of Canada's territory in the northern Pacific area.
I suggest also that there should be at least a division of the reserve army trained to the point where it could take the field in a short space of time. We older soldiers can think only in terms of divisions. It may be that we are out of date and that a division is not the proper unit under present conditions. In any event I believe there should be a substantial group in the reserve army told that they would be the first part of that reserve army to get into the fighting, and they should be trained and equipped accordingly.
This would be much on the basis of the selection of the first division in the recent war. In British Columbia there was only one regiment taken into the first division, the Seaforth Highlanders of Canada, a regiment of which we are justly very proud. There were other excellent regiments in British Columbia, but the Seaforths were picked,
I believe, well in advance of the fighting, as the regiment from British Columbia to go with the first division.
In depending on the reserve army as a whole-we were told in 1946 it would be six divisions-to back up the permanent brigade, we are not being realistic. We should have some designated force prepared to take the
Supply-National Defence field within a very short period of time if trouble comes. Incidentally it would be interesting to know how long the minister thinks it would take for Canada to field a division or similar body of men under present conditions.
With regard to the navy, I submit that there must be an adequate number of ships on the Pacific coast to deal with submarines, and that steps should be taken to protect our harbours. Now is the time to make the arrangements necessary for the protection of the harbours on the Pacific coast. I forgot one suggestion about the army which I had intended to make. There should be an expansion of the Canadian militia rangers. I do not think the minister has mentioned them so far in the debate. As hon. members know, there was set up during the last war on the west coast a body known as the Pacific coast militia rangers. They were not very popular with the army staffs, because they were woodsmen and men accustomed to the sea, first-class outdoor men, but they were not of the disciplined type. It took quite a while for the army staff to get the idea that this force might be of some help if the Japanese invaded the west coast. The morale of the force was excellent. I have never seen anything finer since the days of the Canadian corps in the first war. They were in all the hamlets up and down the west coast and right into the interior. They were very proud of the part they were playing, and if there had been an invasion they would have been of inestimable value to Canada.
Eventually arrangements were made to carry on an establishment of that type in peacetime. I do not know what the strength is at the present time, but I think the Department of National Defence might well consider expanding that force and setting up units not only in British Columbia but also in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. They would be excellent leaders in any guerrilla type of warfare.
I believe also that steps should be taken on the west coast without delay to set up a civil defence system. I read to the committee an extract indicating that the United States have been doing that since early this year, and I believe a beginning should be made as quickly as possible on the west coast of Canada.
Looking a little further afield in the Pacific area, I believe Canada has so much to gain, and nothing to lose, from a Pacific defence pact that no time should be lost in bringing it about. The people on the Pacific coast will suffer most if there is another world war. If there is trouble we are going to need help

Supply-National Defence badly from all our friends on the shores of the Pacific. I am afraid that Canada hangs back too much on this question of a Pacific defence pact. Yesterday I saw a dispatch from Canberra, Australia, in the Ottawa Journal indicating that Australia would join the United States in a Pacific pact. The article reads:
Percy Spender, external affairs minister, said today Australia is ready to join the United States in a Pacific defence pact even if no other countries go along.
If there should be trouble, Canada will need the help of Australia, New Zealand, and other Pacific countries. Our two sister nations are not members of the North Atlantic council. They were not asked to sign the treaty, and there should be the same kind of arrangement for the Pacific.
Another sign which makes me wonder whether the Canadian government is being realistic about the Pacific is the delay in getting a statement about southeast Asia from the Minister of Fisheries who has just returned from Australia. I do not blame him. He made statements when he was in Sydney indicating what he was going to recommend to the Canadian government. It was stated that Canada would likely be making some contribution to help the countries of southeast Asia. On different occasions we have asked for a statement, but there has been delay. Yesterday the Minister of Fisheries said he would have to wait until the estimates of external affairs were under consideration. I hope the difficulty is not that he has met opposition in the cabinet, that there are some members of the cabinet who are taking the position that no help is needed, and that Canada need not become involved in that area.
From what the Minister of Fisheries has said I am convinced that he is in favour of Canada taking action. The same applies to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, because one need only read his speech made earlier in the session, reporting on his trip to the Pacific, to be reassured with regard to his attitude. I urge the Minister of National Defence as strongly as I possibly can that he support these two ministers in cabinet council in urging that Canada announce quickly what she is going to do to help those countries which are trying to stand off communism. I urge him that he see to it that there is an estimate put through the house before the end of the session. If that is not done I do not see how it will be possible to give a great deal of help. I am sure that members of the house would approve such an estimate, but I am worried about the delay. I am afraid that time is of vital importance in the Pacific; that the sands are running out against


us in the Pacific area, and that in the event of trouble Canada will be the nation to suffer most.
As I said in opening, these suggestions are placed before the minister with a pretty clear realization of the difficulties he and the Department of National Defence are facing so soon after they have been through the second world war. Nevertheless that is the position. They, the members of the house and the Canadian people can only meet these sobering problems with courage. I am sure that will be the attitude of the Canadian people as a whole.

I should like to discuss with the minister for a while the question of military morale. In the course of the discussion I might depart considerably from orthodox methods of carrying on debate in the House of Commons, but under the circumstances I believe that what I shall endeavour to do will be justified.
I believe that all hon. members will agree that in order for a nation to fight effectively, it has to have faith: faith in itself, faith in its cause, and faith in its country's future. What I have to say pertains to the development of faith in our people. We are living in an age in which men, in many cases, are losing faith. A large number of the people with whom I speak find themselves bewildered and disheartened. If I might contribute to some extent to the rejuvenation of some of their courage I would consider it worth while, and I believe that you, Mr. Chairman, would also consider it worth while.

Many hon. members, justifiably I believe, are gloomily forecasting that in all probability Canada will be the cockpit of the next war; in other words, that Canada will be the Belgium of world war III.

And I will call for a sword against him throughout all my mountains, saith the Lord God: every man's sword shall be against his brother.

On May 22, when in Worcester, England, he received the freedom of that city, Reuters carried the following report:
Winston Churchill, receiving the freedom of Worcester city, Saturday publicly expressed his distress that "Rule Britannia" had been abolished in the Royal Canadian Navy. The Conservative party leader said:	"It was with a bitter pang that I read
in a newspaper that the Canadian navy had abolished 'Rule Britannia' as the tune to be sung on Canadian ships.
It seems to be a very great pity to sever links with the past so full of lustre as that expressed by the words 'Rule Britannia'."
There be those, and I have heard some say it, who say: "Well, it was none of his business whatsoever to interfere in Canadian affairs." I submit that he was not interfering in Canadian affairs. He was just indicating his own feelings to his own people. It was an involuntary cry of pain from Britain-Britain, always our surest guard, our surest recourse in time of danger, ever since we first began to be.
Men in our time are likely to underestimate the importance of spiritual values. We are engaged in a desperate struggle between belief and non-belief, between belief in God and atheism.
Atheism suggests communism. We have had a number of members rise in this house and cry out against communism. May I suggest that one of the ways to offset communism is to teach people to believe in God. I have never heard anyone suggest in the house up to the present time that that ought to be done. I suggest that it is time that we did it.
Internationalism tends to atheism. There will be those who believe in internationalism who will be shocked by that remark. As evidence that internationalism tends to atheism, I suggest that you read the records pertaining to the San Francisco conference; read the whole United Nations documents;


read the accounts of Bretton Woods, Dumbarton Oaks; read the accounts of all the trade conferences; read the accounts of the Atlantic pact. Do you find any reference in them to God? After reading these documents you would think that we had managed to divorce God from the universe.
You rarely hear anyone in our house refer to God when he rises to speak. If I may say so without casting any reflection on hon. members, I would ask how many of them seem to consider it worth while to come in here and listen to the beautiful prayer which is offered by the Speaker every day, calling for the assistance of Almighty God to be with us in our endeavours to cope with our problems. I will not say anything about it; I will just let hon. members come in and count them for themselves a week or two and see just what the situation is. I do not think it indicates very much attention to the important factor of God in our affairs.
I am not a colonialist; I am not an imperialist; I am merely one who desires to preserve the precious heritage of our British people's past-and no people in the world today has anything like as glorious a past as have the British people.

And I will bless them that bless thee,-
And this is God speaking to Abraham.
-and curse him that curseth thee: and in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed.
If we are descendants of Abraham-and we are; every person in this House of Commons at the present time I believe is a descendant of Abraham-then, there is the beginning of the covenant that makes us covenant men.
Now may I turn to Genesis, chapter 49, verses 22 to 26. Here Jacob, before dying, is blessing his son Joseph. We read:
22.	Joseph is a fruitful bough, even a fruitful bough by a well; whose branches run over the wall:
23.	The archers have sorely grieved him, and shot at him, and hated him:
24.	But his bow abode in strength, and the arms of his hands were made strong by the hands of the mighty God of Jacob; (from thence is the shepherd, the stone is Israel:)
25.	Even by the God of thy father, who shall help thee; and by the Almighty, who shall bless thee with blessings of heaven above, blessings of the deep that lieth under, blessings of the breasts, and of the womb;
26.	The blessings of thy father have prevailed above the blessings of my progenitors unto the utmost bound of the everlasting hills: they shall be on the head of Joseph, and on the crown of the head of him that was separate from his brethren.
There is scarcely a member in the house today who is not a descendant of Joseph. In other words here is a blessing which pertains to us, to our race, to our nation, French speaking and English speaking.
