I turn now to Genesis, chapter 48, verses 14 to 20, which read:
And Israel stretched out his right hand, and laid it upon Ephraim's head, who was the younger, and his left hand upon Manasseh's head, guiding his hands wittingly; for Manasseh was the firstborn.
And he blessed Joseph, and said, God, before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac did walk, the God which fed me all my life long unto this day,
The Angel which redeemed me from all evil, bless the lads; and let my name be named on them, and the name of my fathers Abraham and Isaac; and let them grow into a multitude in the midst of the earth.
And when Joseph saw that his father laid his right hand upon the head of Ephraim, it displeased him: and he held up his father's hand, to remove it from Ephraim's head unto Manasseh's head.
And Joseph said unto his father, Not so, my father: for this is the firstborn; put thy right hand upon his head.
And his father refused, and said, I know it, my son, I know it: he also shall become a people, and he also shall be great: but truly his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his seed shall become a multitude of nations.
And he blessed them that day, saying, In thee shall Israel bless, saying, God make thee as Ephraim and as Manasseh: and he set Ephraim before Manasseh.
I venture to say that there is hardly an hon. member of this house who is not a descendant of Ephraim. In other words, this nation of ours, this Canada, is young Ephraim. But what does it mean? First of all, may I point out that in the verses which I read a promise is made to Ephraim that he shall become a multitude of nations. Will hon. members tell me where in all the world's history there is anything which comes so near to fulfilling that prophecy, that his seed shall become a multitude of nations, as does the British commonwealth of nations? Yet there are people in this country, and apparently in the minister's department, who would destroy that wonderful fulfilment of the promise given to Ephraim.
I think I shall take a few minutes to show something of what it means to us that the British commonwealth is Ephraim. I turn to Jeremiah, chapter 31, verse 9, where the Lord speaking, says:
They shall come with weeping, and with supplications will I lead them; I will cause them to walk by the rivers of waters in a straight way, wherein they shall not stumble; for I am a father to Israel, and Ephraim is my firstborn.
In other words those Ephraimite people who constitute the British commonwealth of nations are the firstborn, the Lord's especially chosen people. In abolishing "Rule Britannia" I wonder if it was intended that we should turn our back on all these wonderful blessings, which the Lord, in the passage of Jeremiah which I have just read, implied for us? Those who want some source of comfort for the days that are to come should


gather a great deal from that passage. I should like now to quote Jeremiah 51, verses 19 to 21 as follows:
The portion of Jacob is not like them; for he is the former of all things: and Israel is the rod of his inheritance: the Lord of hosts is his name.
Thou art my battle axe and weapons of war: for with thee will I break in pieces the nations, and with thee will I destroy kingdoms;
And with thee will I break in pieces the horse and his rider; and with thee will I break in pieces the chariot and his rider;
There is a remarkable promise. We have seen abundant evidence of its fulfilment in world war I, in world war II and in the wars of the nineteenth century. Why are we not trusting the Lord in the times yet to come? Why should we abolish the hymn "Rule Britannia"?
I turn now to one more passage of scripture. Jeremiah 30, verse 11, reads:
For I am with thee, saith the Lord, to save thee: though I make a full end of all nations whither I have scattered thee, yet will I not make a full end of thee: but I will correct thee in measure, and will not leave thee altogether unpunished.
Tell me where there is a nation on the face of this earth that has a finer promise than that. That promise is made to the British people concerning whom "Rule Britannia" was written. Do we want to participate in that promise? I think we do.
May I turn briefly now to some recent British history? Everyone will recall that the Israelites went out of the land of Egypt into the land of Palestine. They remained there for some time and finally they took Saul as their king. They went on to develop under Saul and David and Solomon. After Solomon there was a rebellion, as the result of which Israel was divided into, two kingdoms. The first, consisting of ten tribes, was in the north; the second, consisting of two tribes, was in the south. The tribes in the north took the name of Israel or Ephraim because that was the name of their chief tribe; those in the south took the name of Judah as Judah was their chief tribe.
In 721 B.C. the northern kingdom was carried away into Assyrian captivity, the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh being among them. Later these tribes went away into the north and became the Lost Tribes. Ephraimites and Manassehites in considerable numbers found their way into Britain and Britain grew from them. Probably there will be those who will not accept that story, but I think the evidence upon which it is based is dependable. I would be glad to talk it over personally with anyone who is interested. Thus we have a summary of the history of the British. Several times we have had people agitate in this house for the abolition of the union jack from our flag.

Let us see what these people want to abolish from our flag. I should like to go briefly into the scientific background of the whole subject of the union jack so that we shall be able to see that those who cling to old British traditions are not mere sentimentalists.
What is the meaning of the union jack? Well, the expression "union jack" means the union of Jacob, it means Jacob's flag, the flag which would be flown by the Israelites, by the descendants of Jacob.
What does the union jack consist of? It is made up of three Christian crosses. Many of our French Canadian compatriots, for whom I have the highest degree of admiration, have risen in their places in this house and asked that the union jack be eliminated from our flag. In doing that they are asking that these three Christian crosses be eliminated from our flag. This is the only flag on the face of the earth that is made up entirely of Christian crosses. It is the most Christian flag on the face of the earth. There is no gainsaying that statement. The next time they want to abolish the union jack from the flag of Canada it would be well for them to remember that fact, and also some of the things I am going to suggest to them.
There is a fine scientific treatment of this whole matter to be found in a book entitled "Tracing our Ancestors" by Frederick Haber-man which was copyrighted in the United States in 1934. The book is published by the Kingdom Press of St. Petersburg, Florida, U.S.A. Here is a passage taken from the frontispiece:	.
Ancient pattern for the Union Jack and the Star Spangled Banner.
The Topez of the Sachi:
A rock carving near Bhopal in India of the 4th century B.C.
Taken from Roberts "British History Traced." (See Chapter XI.)
These words are taken from under the picture on the frontispiece of the book. Some hon. members will be astounded to know that in Bhopal, India, there is a big stone, upon which are carved drapes of the union jack and the stars and stripes, the date of the stone being 450 years before Christ. At the bottom of the picture is the unicorn and the lion!
A good many members will find it bard to believe that our history goes back as far as that. The information is taken from Roberts' "British History Traced", chapter 11, according to Mr. Haberman.
The book "Tracing our Ancestors" is respectfully dedicated to President Franklin D. Roosevelt in these words:
In the hope that it will help him in guiding our nation through this period of chaos and transi-55946-217

tion-by explaining the true origin of our race, our mission, and our destiny.
Anyone who desires to be much enlightened on all matters pertaining to Great Britain will do well to read this great work, "Tracing our Ancestors", several times and also to read "Israel-Britain" by Adam Rutherford 1939. May we turn to certain aspects of the union jack? First of all take the transverse cross of St. Andrew of Scotland. This flag, when it stood alone, consisted of a white cross on a blue background with the transverse cross shaped like an X. Where did it come from? What is this transverse cross that the Scottish people loved so dearly? At page 46 "Tracing our Ancestors" has this to say:
It is by means of this battle axe or hammer that Thor, a Gothic deity spoken of also as Indiri the Divine, overcame his enemies and the devil. Thor's hammer is shown to be composed of four bolts and reference to those bolts is also made in the Indian Vedas, where we read:
With thy Spiky Weapon, thy deadly Bolt,
O Indra, thou smotest the Dragon in the face.
Much information concerning this whole matter is given in Professor Waddell's fine book, "Aryan Origin of the Alphabet". Professor Waddell further shows that the name of St. Andrew, the patron saint of the Goths and the Scots, is derived from the word Indra or Indara. Thus the story of St. Andrew and his typical X-shaped cross or weapon is simply a legendary form of the story of Jehovah. In other words, the white cross on the union jack against a blue background is the emblem of Jehovah himself. That white cross represents the weapon with which he beat the dragon. It is one of the crosses composing the union jack!
St. George's red cross, the upright cross representing the cross on which Christ was crucified, also has a most interesting history which I am not going to go into in detail. My object now is not to be exhaustive but merely to give enough detail to suggest that there is some sense behind the attitude of many of us towards Great Britain and the union jack. It is not all sentimentality. The stories of St. George's cross and St. Patrick's cross are just as interesting, just as impressive and just as faith inspiring as is that of St. Andrew's cross. All three are combined in the union jack.
Let us contrast the union jack with the hammer and sickle. Ranged on the side of Great Britain you are ranged against such a mundane emblem as the hammer and sickle which stand for materialism pure and simple. Those people who are so active in their efforts to design a new flag for Canada should take their new designs and contrast them with the union jack with all it signifies over thousands of years of history. Contrast the union jack as an emblem under which to fight, under
3428	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence which to live, under which to die and under which to lie in your grave, with any other flag on earth today, or any other flag you can conceive! You will not find any other flag to compare with the union jack.
"Rule Britannia" recalls the British flag, the union jack. In abolishing it we are turning our backs on the union jack, not of course overtly but by implication.
Great Britain has always been the champion of freedom. Parliament originated in Britain. In 1215 the British fought and won Magna Carta from King John. We have plenty of trouble right now maintaining the rights that were guaranteed under Magna Carta. We bring in a wide variety of high sounding recommendations about human rights, fundamental freedoms and all the rest of it. They won habeas corpus and trial by jury in 1215. Since that time Britons have insisted that they enjoy those rights. "Rule Britannia" recalls the great achievements for freedom made by Great Britain. The very words "Britons never shall be slaves" emphasize that.
"Rule Britannia" suggests Britain's future. We do not know what it will be except from what the prophets say. We have already established the fact that the British are Israelites and Ephraimites. The quotation I have given from scripture indicates what the Lord is going to do with them. He says, "Though I make a full end of all nations, whither I have scattered thee, yet will I not make a full end of thee".

The whole problem of national defence is something that cannot be dealt with secondhand because it is so involved and so technical. If there is the question of the use of a new weapon, if there is the question of the use of the air arm, if there is the question of the expenditure on, shall we say, atomic warheads, the proper people to have that information are the technical advisers in the defence services. The minister gets the information from his advisers. He gets it secondhand. He must get it secondhand because no minister, no single person, can carry that information in his head. It is impossible. The question of national defence is so involved that, even in dealing with the one question of uniformity of the code of discipline that this bill dealt with, we had no fewer than five persons to answer various questions put to them by the committee. They were in constant attendance while the committee was sitting. That was efficiency. That was not having a question asked and the minister asking his experts in front of him. They have a great deal of the information, but they cannot give as detailed and as factual information as could the actual staff officers who will have to deal with the operation of the department and probably with the use of the weapon in question.
An example of that was given this morning in the question of the value of various appreciations of artillery fire and artillery competition. I am not an expert in artillery, but there was certainly left in the minds of the committee some considerable doubt as to the value of these various types of competitions. If we had a senior artillery officer who could answer the questions immediately and give the factual details about the problem facing modern artillery, it would be to the advantage of all. The minister cannot do that. The minister must get his information secondhand. The minister could go and see artillery being


fired; but with all due respect, I submit that he does not know as much about it as the men and the officers who are actually doing the work, using the weapons.
To deal with a matter such as this we need the best possible advice. There is no question of secrecy. If there are new weapons on the secret lists, that fact can be stated. Mention can be made of the fact that they are on the secret list, and, as in the national defence committee, nothing further will be discussed in regard to them. But I do want to say again that on this matter of national defence the greatest single item of governmental expense, the thing which may make or break our security and on which our whole life depends, requires the most efficient and effective treatment that this house can possibly give it. I think the other hon. members of the national defence committee will say that the efficiency and the effectiveness of that committee could be copied by this committee of the whole house, and that a great deal of good would come from it.
Unfortunately, I was not here yesterday. In reading over the discussion in Hansard I could not find anything being said about preparation for submarine warfare. I am not now referring to antisubmarine warfare, because that is one of our principal tasks. Today, whether we like it or not in any future conflict, no matter what the new weapons and weapons of mass structure are, one of the jobs that Canada will have to do will be the job of transportation, We will have to continue to keep the sea lanes open between ourselves and our allies, particularly on the Atlantic. Today the air arm is being stressed, but with the new weapons the underwater arm, the submarine arm, has assumed almost equal importance with the air arm. With the tremendous speed of the modern submarine, with the enormously improved hitting powers of the modern torpedo, with the tremendously increased distance that can be travelled at very much greater speed, the submarine is not only an offensive weapon of the first magnitude, but a defensive weapon of equal power. We are vulnerable with an enormous sea coast, vulnerable in our harbours, vulnerable also to the atomic weapon used under water. We have apparently decided not to embark on the construction or bringing into force of a submarine arm of the navy at all. I mentioned this before. I still feel that the submariner is one of the most important warriors of the future.
I should like to ask the minister whether it is on account of costs, whether it is on account of our shipbuilding industry, or

what are the reasons that we have not embarked upon this type of warfare. The major countries of the world, including Russia, the United States and the United Kingdom are concentrating more and more upon the submarine as a weapon. Apparently however that is not the policy of this administration. Perhaps there are good reasons for this; perhaps we have not embarked upon it because of costs. But the submarine nearly beat us in 1916-17, and came even closer to beating us in the last war. It seems to me that to neglect this weapon, which so nearly destroyed us, is not realistic. I should remind the house that the first submarines to cross the Atlantic were built in Canada. We cannot train, we cannot build, we cannot produce a submarine force in a short time. It is expensive, as are all matters connected with defence. But if we are met with this problem after war has broken out time will be our enemy. Now time is on our side, and I would therefore ask the minister what consideration has been given to this matter and what are the reasons for failing to embark upon this particular phase of naval warfare.
We do not know whether the weapons of mass destruction, particularly the hydrogen bomb, can be produced. But from every authority, including the Secretary of War in the United States, it seems pretty well established that the hydrogen bomb can and will be produced. There is no need to be unduly depressing; but if these can be released and can be detonated-if that is the correct term when speaking of fissionable material-then whole tracts of country and hundreds of thousands or even millions of people will be destroyed, not by the explosion itself but by the radioactive effect left on the contaminated ground by this new weapon. That is something to which consideration should be given. Just how far the matter has been considered, I do not know. Perhaps the minister will say what has been and what is being done in connection with atomic warfare. This is something in which the civilian population will have to take part. Let us not fool ourselves: there will be no scruples on the part of any enemy to refrain from using the weapons of mass destruction.
In the United Nations we pass pious resolutions about genocide. Believe me, there will be no adherents to that resolution if another war breaks out.

I might say, since the hon. member has expressed interest in it before, that at the present time we have more trained paratroopers in Canada than landed in the low Countries in the German invasion in May, 1940.

As a matter of fact, the picture was considerably exaggerated. The actual number of paratroopers and airborne troops that were landed was discovered after the German capitulation when the commander in chief of the German airborne army was interrogated. The details of that interrogation are to be found in a book by Liddell Hart, who was chief military commentator for the London Times before the war and is one of the best known military experts and writers on military matters. In his book called "The Other Side of the Hill" he gives details of the interrogation

which show that the actual number of German paratroopers landed in Holland was 4,500, with another 500 being landed in Belgium, making a total of 5,000 for the low countries. In addition- one airborne division of 12,500 men was landed.
As I say, I find it extremely difficult to accept the fact that we have 5,000 trained paratroopers. That would be more than the number of men that would be trained as paratroopers in our mobile brigade group if that brigade group were completely up to strength, which it is not. The people trained as paratroopers are chiefly infantry men. There are infantry battalions in our brigade group and if all the men were trained-I know they are not-you would have a total of only 1,800. In addition to that there would be signallers, engineers, a limited number of artillery men who would act as forward observation officers, and other personnel of that sort. If the artillery is to be landed and is to be effective it must be from gliders or planes, and the same thing with the armoured corps people. Under those circumstances I find it extremely difficult to accept the minister's statement.
Statements of that sort do a great deal of damage. I know the minister has no intention of deliberately misinforming the house or the country, but it so happens that that particular statement has been given wide publicity in the newspapers and over the air. To put out the idea that we have more trained paratroopers than the Germans dropped on Holland and Belgium in May 1940 is just ridiculous. It creates a false impression as to our defence situation.
This is the type of thing-I think it is unintentional in most cases-which the minister does quite frequently. This morning the leader of the opposition brought up the matter of artillery training. There are two or three other incidents which I shall refer to later, but I simply wanted to point out that it is absolutely useless, as far as giving information to this house is concerned, to make statements such as that.
The general public do not know just how many paratroopers the Germans did drop, but the general idea is that it was tens of thousands. Therefore the statement is misleading from that point of view. I am quite convinced that we do not have over 5,000 trained paratroopers and I doubt whether the minister will maintain that we do have that many. My remarks would apply also to statements setting out percentages, to show that the percentage of personnel in the navy was greater than in any other country. That gives a wrong impression to the general public who do not have any detailed

knowledge of these things. I think it is time we got away from statements of that kind and were given some definite information which would outline the picture as it is. I wish the minister would comment on the paratroop statement which he made yesterday.

. . . our defence has never been envisaged as the defence of Canada alone but the defence of Canada as part of a continent, and indeed the defence of Canada as part of the defence of the western countries which would all be involved in the event of a war for our freedom.
A little further down on the same page the minister said:
But we do not believe it will have any immediate or very considerable effect on our own defence forces, because our defence planning has envisaged the operation of our defences in conjunction with other nations at all times.
At page 3376 he is reported as saying:
... I told the house then, as I tell the committee now, that we have not.
That is, no specific military commitments.
I am not too sure that the North Atlantic treaty organization will ever develop in a way in which there are specific military commitments. That remains to be seen. It remains to be worked out.
I point out to the minister that the statements by the United States military authorities are at variance with the statements made by him in discussing the effect of over-all defence strategy under the Atlantic treaty and similar mutual defence arrangements. Taking the minister's statements that I have just quoted and analysing them, it surely must become obvious that there is an effect or ought to be an effect on Canada's planning because if we have envisaged the operation of our defence in conjunction with other nations at all times, we have reached the stage now where the other Atlantic pact nations with whom we are associated are assuming certain definite responsibilities themselves with respect to the elements of the joint force they are going to contribute. If they are doing that then surely we are in a position, and certainly should be, of making up our minds as to the elements of the joint force that we

Supply-National Defence are going to contribute, and particularly making plans as to the role in the over-all strategical concept which Canada must discharge.
Looking at the white paper on defence we find we are in the very humiliating position of referring at length in our statement on defence policy to what the Americans have said is their concept of the role of the United States in the mutual defensive arrangements which are being made, and at the same time we have no indication of what is Canada's role under these mutual defensive arrangements. We have to look to the pronouncements of the United States chiefs of the joint staffs to find any indication as to what arrangements have been made and what responsibilities have been accepted by any of the members of the mutual defensive arrangement with regard to the problem of joint defence. It is still too early to spell out the consequences of the pact in terms of men and dollars. One thing must be emphasized: the North Atlantic treaty is a pact for peace. Its final result will not be to increase the expenditures which every nation on our side must make. By pooling resources, the effect of the pact should be to reduce the total expenditures which each of the twelve countries would have found necessary for their security had there been no pact. However, that result is some distance off and in the meantime, Canada will have to make such modification of her plans as may be found necessary to meet the situation. While the North Atlantic treaty makes for security, it will only be effective in so far as it represents a pooling of strength rather than a dilution of strength.
We are told in the high sounding statements which have been made in the house with respect to the communique after the joint meeting in London that decisions of vital and far-reaching importance with respect to the over-all defence planning have been taken. If that is the case, then surely we are entitled to take the words at their face value. But assuming that those decisions are what they are said to be, decisions of far-reaching importance, and that progress is being made in the planning of joint defence under the pact, then the answer the minister made last night, that it has no effect upon our defence strategy, is at variance with his earlier statement in the white paper that the Atlantic pact will have an effect in reducing the total expenditure which each of the twelve countries would have found necessary if there had been no pact.


This white paper goes on to analyse the defence implications, and those are the words used, with respect to the Atlantic treaty. It says:
At the meeting of defence ministers on October 5 the north Atlantic nations requested that the regional groups should complete their organization early in November.
That is eight months ago.
Strategical planning will then be undertaken by representatives of the nations in each group. Those plans will be co-ordinated by the military committee standing group composed of representatives of the chiefs of staff of France, the United Kingdom and the United States. In this way there will be prepared an over-all strategical plan with an indication of its requirements and how they will be met. Requirements of equipment will be referred to the military production and supply board. Reports on progress will be made at the second meeting of the defence committee.
I wish particularly to emphasize the words, "In this way there will be prepared an over-all strategical plan with an indication of its requirements and how they will be met." Canada, as a member of the North Atlantic treaty, must obviously, in view of the statements which have recently been made with regard to collective security and balanced forces, be prepared to meet certain requirements when those requirements have been laid down. Again, unless we are being told that the decisions taken at London were not of such importance as has previously been indicated, then we can only assume that decisions along the lines of what would be the joint requirements have been taken, and we are therefore entitled to be told what their effect is upon Canada's defence strategy.
Then the white paper continues:
While the strategy of the north Atlantic powers has not yet been formally stated, our participation in planning for the defence of this continent and of the western union gives a clear indication of the main lines of strategy though they may not have been put into words. Our planning has been flexible and can be adapted to any responsibilities we may assume.
This passage clearly indicates that the western union, which is another name for the north Atlantic alliance, will have a definite strategical plan, or has one. Canada, as part of that alliance, must undertake certain responsibilities with respect to carrying out that strategical plan. We want to know what the effects of that are upon our defence planning at home.
It is interesting to note, Mr. Chairman, that immediately following this section in the white paper outlining the defence implications of the North Atlantic pact, there is a lengthy statement quoted from General Bradley's testimony before the foreign affairs committee of the house of representatives on July 29, 1949. His statement was made during the hearings on the Mutual Defence

Assistance Act of 1949. Is it important to realize where this comes in the context, because this statement of General Bradley is quoted immediately following the purported analysis of the defence implications of the North Atlantic treaty. It can only be taken therefore, as indeed is obvious, as implying that General Bradley's statement on the Mutual Defence Assistance Act is immediately related to the over-all strategical plan under the north Atlantic alliance. The minister tells us that he cannot say what the effect of the Atlantic treaty on Canada is. He cannot outline any responsibility which we have assumed, or any commitments which we may be prepared or preparing to consider. It is significant that General Bradley goes into clear and concise detail as to the responsibilities which the United States might have assumed under this over-all defence set-up. It is significant to note that General Bradley gives his outline to the foreign affairs committee of the house of representatives. He stated:
In our approach to this arms-aid program, the joint chiefs of staff have followed the principle that the man in the best position, and with the capability, should do the job for which he is best suited.
Further, our recommendations-
That is the recommendations of the joint chiefs of staff to the government of the United States.
-for this program have been predicated upon this basic principle, and the following assumed factors:
First, the United States will be charged with the strategic bombing.
We have repeatedly recognized in this country that the first priority of the joint defence is our ability to deliver the atomic bomb.
Second, the United States navy and the western union naval powers will conduct essential naval operations, including keeping the sea lanes clear. The western union and other nations will maintain their own harbour and coastal defence.
Third, we recognize that the hard core of the ground power in being will come from Europe, aided by other nations as they can mobilize.
Fourth, England, France, and the closer countries will have the bulk of the short-range attack bombardment, and air defence. We, of course, will maintain the tactical air force for our own ground and naval forces, and United States defence.
Then he goes on to outline other considerations and specific undertakings or responsibilities assumed by the United States in connection therewith.
I want to close by saying that General Bradley, who is head of the joint chiefs of staff committee, has indicated clearly the responsibilities of the United States under this overall defence arrangement. In Canada we have had no such indication. In the United States, General Bradley gives his evidence before a committee of the house of representatives. We are told that this committee of the whole is the only committee we will have, so we cannot 55946-218

I for one am not content to believe that is the case. I am therefore more dissatisfied with the minister's failure to make a clear statement to this committee in answer to our questions as to the effect upon Canada's defence planning of the recent decisions taken under the North Atlantic pact.

I should like to tell the minister that I feel he is handling the situation well. I have listened carefully to the questions. I think the Conservatives have done a good job in questioning the minister and I believe he has done a good job in 5594G-218?.
Supply-National Defence answering. My own feeling is that our defence is in good hands and being taken care of. The minister has my confidence in that respect. I am sure he will justify it.
Before closing my remarks a bit earlier in the afternoon I wanted to make one or two comments that I do think are important at the present time. I wanted to say that whereas there are a great many people who believe that our security is to be found in international agreements I do not concur in that view. I think we shall find that the more we rely on international agreements the greater will be our disappointments and frustrations in the end. I may be wrong in that. But I want to urge upon the minister that while he co-operates with international organizations such as the Atlantic pact, which thus far could be all to the good, he take the very greatest care to see that nothing is done which will cause Canada to surrender her sovereignty in any respect to any agency which is set up under the Atlantic pact.
The other day we had a discussion of the estimates of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. If one-tenth as much of Canada's sovereignty had been required by Britain even in the war of 1914-18 there would have been a scream that would have rent the skies and torn the stars down. But we calmly accept the most extravagant suggestions as to what we are going to agree to do in obedience to some single individual appointed by the Atlantic pact!
Now, Mr. Chairman, that is serious. I happen to know that for over 75 years certain definite international forces have been aiming at the destruction of the British commonwealth and the establishment of a world state under which no nation will have sovereignty.
I can find on record statements that are unchallengeable, which will prove that such has been designed. I have strong evidence to show that world war I was deliberately designed by these men who aim at this objective. All during that war they carried on their manipulations, their machinations, with the aim of bringing about their objective; and as soon as world war 1 was finished they began to plan world war II with the same object in view. They by that time started talking openly about what their aim was, as I pointed out the other day in the debate on the external affairs estimates, they started telling us about what they were working for as early as 1941 and 1942, and the evidence can be found in great United States magazines. The handwriting is too clear for us to disregard, Mr. Chairman.
If our greatest security, economically, politically and in every other way were to

Supply-National Defence be obtained through such measures I should not find it bad enough; but there is no guarantee whatsoever that that security can be secured or will be secured by such measures, or that the object of these men, who are aiming to build up this world organization, is to provide security. Rather the appearance is that the very opposite is their aim, namely, not to provide security but to make us take what they want to give us and make us like it.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that when the objective of these gentlemen is achieved it will be too late to get up and talk. We shall have given over our sovereignty. That is one reason why I am talking as I am today. I see a genuine danger.
I wish to urge on the minister that while we are ready to co-operate with any person of good will or any number of persons, we are not prepared to surrender one jot of our sovereignty any more than this parliament would have been prepared to surrender any of our sovereignty to Great Britain in 1934 or 1935 when the need for preparation was tremendous, and Great Britain was prepared to offer leadership, but we were everlastingly worrying about how much of our sovereignty we were going to surrender. Let us worry just as much about how much of our sovereignty we are going to surrender to these international people, no matter how high their position may be.
I say again to the minister that while he may work and co-operate with all of these people, I wish him to give careful consideration to this possibility, that the finest organization that we can possibly have, looking toward our political security, our economic security, and every other kind of security that the heart of man desires, is an organization based on the pattern of the British commonwealth, in which there is complete unification of action, but in which there is no surrender of sovereignty whatsoever. The effectiveness of such an organization was amply demonstrated in world wars I and IX, and the effectiveness of such an organization was demonstrated in 1932 when the representatives of the various members of the commonwealth met here in Ottawa and signed the Ottawa agreements as the means of offsetting the economic adversities that were swelling around us.
Why depart from a thing which has served us so satisfactorily on so many occasions during past years? Therefore, I say, let us do everything that can possibly be done to liberate the members of the British commonwealth so that they may be free to act together effectively, and then encourage them so to do. Then let us teach our people that


there is hope in co-operating with the British commonwealth. The quotations which I gave this afternoon, if hon. members find interest in reading them, will be sufficient to show that our faith in the British commonwealth is based on very solid considerations.
We already had autonomous communities within the British commonwealth under the Balfour declaration of 1926. Every hon. member is familiar with what was said. There is no need of repeating it. But while we were completely autonomous communities and Canada, Australia, New Zealand and any other part of the commonwealth was equal in status to Britain, yet we were bound together by considerations of common allegiance to the crown. Not only will a common allegiance to the crown provide a means of binding us together. We can be bound together by such considerations as our common ancestry, which I mentioned this afternoon, and which constitutes one of the reasons for the talk I gave this afternoon. We realize that members of the British commonwealth are blood brothers, in a very real sense. We have a common heritage, which I hinted at this afternoon but barely touched upon. We have a common aim. We have common ideals. We have a common sense of the need for each other's aid in defence and in general economic security. We have a common destiny.
What more do men and nations need to impel them to act together in unity? If we bring about a united nations through the means of the British commonwealth we shall have everything that can possibly be offered by any other group of united nations, and we shall safeguard everything which our race has fought for through thousands of years. I say let us act. Let us British people not barter away our precious birthright, our hard-won heritage.
I should like to commend the Minister of Labour in this connection for the most excellent contribution he made to the debate on June 2, as it appears at page 3151 of Hansard. I do not know when I have heard a more genuinely British speech, and at the same time a more downright Canadian speech, a more genuinely common-sense speech than the one he delivered on that occasion. I wish it could be read into the record right here, in connection with what I have to say.
I suggest to the minister that as the days go by he take steps to restore "Rule Britannia" to be played on the ships of Canada-but not to displace "O Canada". I do not have to be any less an Albertan to be a Canadian. As a matter of fact, generally speaking, the more loyal and passionately devoted I am

to Alberta, the more loyal and passionately devoted I am to Canada; because they are one. We do not have to be any less devoted to Canada in order to be devoted to the commonwealth and the motherland, and to play "Rule Britannia". Let us play them both on the ships.
I suggest to the minister that from now on he resist every effort to have Canada or any other British country surrender any of its sovereignty to any agency outside the British commonwealth, or inside the commonwealth. Everyone says that we do not want in the empire centralized control. What astounds me is that we will turn from making a remark like that and favour centralized control with a lot of people with whom we have in common hardly anything whatsoever. Let us see that we do not do that kind of thing.
I suggest to the minister that he take every step he can take to disseminate knowledge and understanding among our armed forces as to the meaning of these great things we have, our ancestry, our flag, our emblems, our institutions, our ideals. All we have to do is to follow up the kind of study I was indicating this afternoon, and we shall get our armed services to understand that there is a great scriptural and prophetic background behind this British race. They will know then that there is a glorious destiny prophesied for this race, and that it is a wonderful and a joyful thing for all of us to co-operate to attain that noble destiny.
I suggest that all men in our time should be constantly on the alert lest they put forth unhallowed hands to desecrate sacred things.

He knows that the brigade group has an establishment of something in excess of 5,000, and I have told him that it is approximately 80 per cent up to strength. The formation with regard to that was the one bit of information to which I referred before and for which he had asked in the house. On the advice of my advisers I told him that it was not in the public interest to give information about the actual strength and the state of training of individual formations, particularly of the brigade group, because that group represented the means we have of defending ourselves against such attacks as might be made suddenly in the way of diversionary or other attacks. It was the piece of information which a potential aggressor would most want to have. It is the one piece of information which on the advice of my advisers I said that I felt we should not give, and I referred to that yesterday.
With regard to the army, it is difficult to differentiate between the active and reserve forces. As the hon. member knows, a considerable proportion of the active force devotes a large part of its time to reserve force training and activities. A large part of all the training staff in the active force spends its time training the reserve force and yet it appears exclusively in the active force lists and votes. It really is not possible to sort out the functions of the armed forces in the way the hon. member mentions.

This leads up to another question which I asked the minister yesterday and to which I did not get an answer that really covered the , matter. I was referring to section 6 of our defence policy which was enunciated by the minister on November 11, 1949, and which reads:
Since an attack on Canada could only be made by air or by sea, emphasis must be placed on defence forces; by air-radar stations and communications, backed by interceptors and a relatively small mobile brigade group;
Yesterday I asked the minister if we had those radar stations and communications, backed by interceptors and a brigade group capable of doing the task which he himself has said was necessary in preventing diversionary raids and things of that sort. In dealing with Exercise Sweetbriar in March the minister stated that our defending forces should be able to prevent an attacker leapfrogging from airport to airport. I asked whether or not we have sufficient interceptors and trained men in the brigade group to prevent an enemy leapfrogging from airfield to airfield, but that is another question to which I have not had an answer.
The minister has made quite a point that he has answered every question that has been asked, but he answers a lot of them, such as the two or three I have mentioned, in a way which does not constitute an answer at all. I wonder if the minister could make a statement with
Supply-National Defence reference to the ability of the two interceptor squadrons, the transport planes and the brigade group of about 4,000 men that we have at the present time to prevent an enemy from leapfrogging from airfield to airfield, which he has stated is a necessary thing for us to be able to do.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, May 23, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gillis for second reading of Bill No. 6, to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act (enforcement).

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I believe I adjourned the debate on this motion, Mr. Speaker. I am opposed to this bill for the same reason as I was opposed to the bill introduced by the member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy). I want to make this observation, if I may. There is a wrong conception here of the responsibility of the members on this board. They are not free agents, nor do they represent particular interests. They bring their

talents to the board, and once they are members of the board they are servants of the state carrying out the will of this parliament. I have checked this with the leaders of the British trade union movement, and other countries that follow our form of government. I believe the hon. member, upon reflection, will see that the present machinery is in keeping with the spirit of what he suggests. I say that not critically, but analytically. I must take the same stand I took on the other bill, that this is not a court but a labour relations board.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the motion is put to the house I should like to register my own opposition to this bill. I consider it objectionable. for the reasons which have already been so well explained by the minister on other occasions. My own 'belief is that if this bill were to carry it would strike at the root of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act which, as the house knows, is predicated upon the conciliation of industrial disputes, in addition to its other functions of course.
Since 1944 labour relations have been satisfactorily administered under the wartime labour relations regulations, and since the first of September, 1948, under the present act. Under both the act and the regulations the function of the Minister of Labour was to strive towards the bringing together of management and labour. This has been working satisfactorily. From every quarter in this house, not to speak of high authorities in the ranks of both labour and management inside and outside this country, the achievements of the Department of Labour in the administration of the regulations and the act have been highly praised. I do not think we should hurriedly change the spirit of that act, which has really been the secret of the success which has been achieved.
The act was adopted by this house after thorough consideration by the standing committee on industrial relations during the course of two sessions. I feel therefore that it is wrong to try to change one of the basic features of the act without giving that same committee an opportunity of going over the act once more. After a year and a half of operation, I submit it is premature to consider any such radical change. As a matter of fact not very many complaints have been placed before the minister requesting leave to prosecute. Many of those requests did not result in the issuance of any such consent, because the dispute which was the cause of the request was settled. In only a few exceptional cases was there any occasion for the minister to give
Industrial Relations
his consent to prosecute. Under those circumstances, and without rehashing the reasons that have been given for objecting to the passage of this bill, I believe it is sufficient for me to invite this house to vote against the bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext:
If I may be
privileged, sir, I should like to make one or two observations about this bill. First, sir, I quite realize that those who are charged with the responsibility of labour relations in the province of Ontario are so anxious, so happy, to be able to help labour relations in every possible way. But, sir, as one of the young members of this house, in common with you, I may say that we have seen rapid progress made in labour legislation. I think, sir, that today we have reached the stage where we ought to stop, look and ponder on what has transpired with regard to our labour relations, and be careful not to get too far ahead of ourselves in this country. We should do so for this reason; that the economy of this country, compared with the economy of the rest of civilization, is still in advance of all countries from the standpoint of labour relations. Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, we could inveigle our friend, or persuade him, into letting this particular bill ride over for another year. We are into the hot weather now and we shall be cooler next January or February when the next session comes along. I would ask the hon. member who introduced this bill to give us, please, a chance to check and double check with regard to how far we are going in this country of ours in the matter of labour legislation -yes, in the matter of all kinds of legislation, not just labour legislation alone. In common with other hon. members in this house, I am a labourer in the vineyard, and we are doing the best we can. I seriously ask, Mr. Speaker, that we do not make haste so fast. Let us make haste slowly so that when that haste is made on labour legislation, the legislation will be of a kind that will stick and of a kind that will, in the final analysis, be of great benefit to the major portion of our population, namely, those who produce.
I should like to see this particular bill stand over until another session when we can give it more thought. Do not let us get ahead too fast with this sort of thing.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I am not
going to take more than five minutes, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) will have plenty of time in which to close the debate. I speak now only for a moment in order to confirm the principle which I supported and advocated in another bill a short time ago, that is, that in labour

Industrial Relations
matters, any legislation that has assisted labour in every jurisdiction should be allowed at least a trial and that our courts should be permitted to exercise the jurisdiction granted them by the sections which it is sought to repeal or alter, in order that we may find out how it works. If it fails, then perhaps there might be the necessity for some such legislation as is sought to be passed in this particular bill.
I am anxious to make that statement in order that the hon. member for Cape Breton South will have ample opportunity to answer it; because, strange as it may seem, we are rather friendly and we have had some discussions about this particular thing; and I know that he is anxious to refute the principle which I advocate.
I am going to say something more, still watching my five minutes, Mr. Speaker, and it is this. Something happened the other day which I think is the greatest advance in industrial relations that has happened on this continent in all the years that I can remember. That is the settlement within the past week or ten days of the General Motors strike in the United States. The point I make there is this. It was a five-year settlement. Business could proceed with the knowledge that that problem was settled for that time. I make no comment on whether that settlement was good for labour or good for management. That is something on which I do not express any opinion; but having regard to that five-year basis, which is the longest time in recent years-anyway within my memory

for which a contract of that kind has been made, I say that is a great advance in the relations between management and labour.
I say this also. No one will get any money at all from the operation of a business unless he gets it from the profit dollar which the business makes. Shareholders will not get anything and labour will not get anything unless they get it from that source; because no one is foolish enough to carry on a business for any length of time to the point where he may lose his capital investment. He will adopt some other method of seeking something from the wreck. I think that settlement is a splendid affirmation, both by the management of General Motors and by Walter Reuther and labour. I think it is the first real evidence of a long view being taken by both capital and labour; and I use the word "capital" advisedly because I believe in it and I know of no better name to give it. I think they have accomplished a great deal because, as we know, Mr. Speaker, in numbers this labour organization is certainly the largest one we have on the North American continent. That that difficulty was resolved on a basis of conciliation is, I

think, eloquent proof of the fact that both parties, the shareholders who will be seeking dividends and the labourers who will be seeking wages, have shown, by that positive act, an appreciation of the fact that the business must succeed and make a profit in order that either element or either party to the difficulty which they had may receive anything. We know that they have agreed on an advancing scale of wages year by year to the end of that contract. That is one of the finest expressions that I know of of confidence in business and in our present system of carrying on business.
I find that I have gone one minute beyond the five about which I spoke to you, Mr. Speaker. May I repeat this particularly to my hon. friend who is the sponsor of this bill. May I remind him of the co-operation that we had when this bill was passed after long, interesting and well-attended sessions of a committee of this house; and may I suggest to him that perhaps he should not be in too great a hurry to alter what we did at that time. Irrespective of that, I am one of those who are opposed to taking jurisdiction from the courts, as this does, until we have some proof that the courts have failed in their duty in respect to matters of this kind. I do not want to be technical, but I point out to him that he probably should have provided in his amendment for something which apparently was overlooked, namely, an appeal of some kind from the summary jurisdiction which he seeks to have exercised by the board.
It is true his amendment says that, the labour board having found so and so, you simply place that finding before a magistrate. He calls it a magistrate's court. I may say that in law I do not know that name for a court. It is a court of summary jurisdiction. The bill provides that having placed the finding of the board before that court, then the court may make an order by way of penalty, having regard to what the statute provides, for a breach of the provision which the labour board found the individual or the corporation guilty of.
I am very much afraid that if we were to pass his amendment in its present form there would be nowhere else to go after the board had made its finding, right or wrong. I am not basing my opposition on that. I am merely pointing that out to the hon. member. He may have a complete answer, because I have discovered that in this House of Commons he is one of the practical lawyers, and he certainly has appeared before boards often enough to know. Perhaps the word I should have used is "advocate." I know he is an excellent advocate; but I point out that technical difficulty

to him and ask him in closing the debate to point out whether I am wrong, as it may well be that I am.
I do know that in all matters of summary conviction before summary courts, which are usually courts presided over by a justice of the peace, two justices of the peace or a stipendiary magistrate-that is a big word, sir, but I do not know any other to use; that is what they call them-in every line of endeavour there is always an appeal to a higher authority. I know I am right about that. It may be I am wrong in saying that in this particular instance he has not provided a further opportunity for the accused and convicted person to seek redress.
I have gone beyond my five minutes, but I am sure I have left the hon. member plenty of time to answer the very short observations I have made.

speechtext: I must inform the house that if the hon. member for Cape Breton South speaks now he will close the debate.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I might say nothing at this time, have the house take a vote and have the bill voted down. If there were any danger of its carrying, the bill would likely be talked out; but I am going to take a little time to do something that I have not done to date, namely, explain what I mean by this bill.
When the industrial relations committee discussed the present national labour code I went into this matter very thoroughly before the committee, and the committee did not see its way clear to write this provision into the act.
Just before taking his seat the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) made the observation that perhaps I was in a hurry about this thing. Well, a couple of years have elapsed since the drafting of the code; and if haste is a crime in the matter of amending the code there were many people on the other side of the house in great haste to amend the code as provided by the labour relations committee. We wrote into the labour relations code the check-off clause. When it came before this house, and before the house had a chance to discuss the matters that were written into the code by the committee, an amendment was made in this house that took out of the code the provision that the committee had written in.
If I am exhibiting undue haste in endeavouring to have this clause written in, the precedent was set by the government, and I have waited considerably longer to press a matter that I had strongly emphasized in the committee.
Industrial Relations
At this time I just want to make a few observations on what has been said, namely, someone else's interpretation of what the amendment means. I gave this matter a great deal of consideration. As the hon. member for Calgary West has indicated, I have been before many conciliation boards in the last thirty years. I am not recommending something here that I do not know from practical experience is going to be of great benefit to the future of labour relations in this country.
A few nights ago the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Stewart) waved his arms but said very little as to the bill itself. He made just the old line political attack on the C.C.F. What did he say? You could pick this out of the ravings in the time that he occupied in discussion. He said that labour in this country did not want this bill, that they knew nothing about it. I want to say that the bill was carefully drafted with the assistance of the law officer of the crown who is provided for that purpose. From the legal standpoint I think it meets the requirements. But before we did anything to this bill we called in representatives of the Canadian Congress of Labour. We sat down and discussed this bill clause by clause, and without any reservation they endorsed the bill and said it would be a good thing to have written into the code.
In addition to being an excellent lawyer the hon. member for Calgary West is also a labour advocate of long standing. He has been legal adviser to the united mine workers, district 18, over a good many years. While he sticks religiously to his law as defined by the Criminal Code of Canada, he slips a lot in his philosophy with regard to the labour movement, and indicates that he has not followed as closely as he should the development of provincial law in the matter of labour relations in this country.
We are not asking for anything new. Hon. members who opposed this bill indicate that they have not followed the matter of provincial law very closely. We are a long way behind the provinces on this particular point, because in Canada today every province has a labour relations act, and a labour relations board on a provincial scale, it is equivalent to the national labour code, but more than that it covers many more classifications of labour.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Will my hon. friend give this parliament credit for setting the example?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext:
You are away behind; you should have set this example long ago. But as it is now we are following the provinces, and we should not be doing that. In this matter of enforcing the act, every labour

Industrial Relations
relations board in this country has the right to do what we are trying to enable the national labour board to do here. And if there is any doubt about that, then my hon. friend can just look back to what happened a couple of years ago. At that time the privy council rendered a decision in this matter, as to whether provincial boards had the right to enforce that legislation. That was in connection with the John East Company of Regina against the labour relations board of Saskatchewan. It was decided by the Supreme Court of Canada that they did not have jurisdiction to enforce their legislation. Then the case went to England. The then provincial minister of labour, the Hon. L. D. Currie, who at the present time is a judge of the supreme court of Nova Scotia, attended at the hearing, and backed the Saskatchewan labour relations board. He is a progressive man in that field, and he said that an adverse decision against the Saskatchewan board would mean that it was taking power from the other boards across the country which had been exercising those powers for some time.
Then my hon. friend goes back to the question of stare decisis which I have heard them talk so much about: the decision of the privy council stands. That decision has been made, and it has given jurisdiction to the provincial boards to do this very thing.
My hon. friend is a Conservative in politics. Surely he is not going to take a position in the house against what a Conservative government in Ontario has done on this very question. They were functioning under the national code for some time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: I will accept stare decisis but not "Clarie" decisis.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The parliamentary assistant said a moment ago that this has not been tried. "Just give it a chance. We have not had any disputes recently in this regard or in the provinces. Things are going along pretty well." Well, he had some pretty bad disputes under the old national code, as it was. I am sure he will not say that the Canadian seamen's dispute was not a bad one. I am reasonably sure he will not say that the strike of automotive workers at Windsor a couple of years ago was not a bad one. I am sure he will not say that the mine workers' strike in Nova Scotia a few years ago, which lasted five months, was not a bad one. All those strikes at that time came under the supervision of the Department of Labour here in Ottawa.
Since Ontario has set up its own act, and has benefited by the difficulties of the past in regard to labour relations and authority in

that field, they have written a code of their own. Since they wrote that code of their own they have provided machinery that gives the necessary authority to the minister of labour, provincially, to get in there, and, through his power, to prevent strikes.
That is what I am aiming at here. I do not suppose there is' anyone in the House of Commons who went through more strikes when we had no legislation. I take a back seat to no one in this country today in my desire to prevent strikes, because strikes are like wars: no one wins; everyone loses.
I want to see legislation in this country that not only gives responsibility to bodies like the national labour board or provincial labour boards, but I want to see such bodies having the necessary authority to carry out their functions. The national board has not that authority at this time.
For the benefit of the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith), who is a Conservative in politics, and who, I am sure, will not disagree with the Conservative government of Ontario, let me place on record a short synopsis of the provincial statute on this very point of the authority to prosecute:
The Ontario labour relations board will have power to decide if a conciliation board is required in a dispute and to authorize prosecutions for unfair labour practices. These powers formerly were held by the minister.
That is exactly the position the national labour relations board and the minister are in today. The minister now has supreme authority in matters of prosecution. Regardless of what employers or employees or the national labour relations board may think in the matter of a prosecution, they must get permission from the Minister of Labour. I say that is unfair to the minister, and places in his hands dictatorial powers he should not have. Personally, I would not want it.
Last Sunday night I listened to a reporter from the Press Gallery give a news round-up from Ottawa. I would advise him to get in touch with somebody, or to get a little book on labour relations and the functions of national and provincial boards, as well as conciliation boards. He broadcast at some length on this particular point, and said, "Oh, that is asking for judicial power for every conciliation board across this country." For his benefit let me say that this has nothing to do with conciliation boards. If he was not any better informed in respect to the rest of his subjects that night than he was on this one, I would advise him to get another job, rather than attempt to interpret the news to the Canadian people.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: What were his other subjects?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Markets, international affairs,
and that kind of thing. But if he did not understand something that has been discussed in the House of Commons a good many times, and discussed in a committee I have seen him attend-and I refer to the labour relations committee-then I say we cannot accept his advice very seriously on such matters as marketing, international affairs and so on.
This particular bill has nothing to do with conciliation boards. The parliamentary assistant said that this question has never been brought up since the adoption of the code. The matter has been tested. He could check back and And the case of the Hull Transportation Commission v. the Canadian Congress of Labour. That particular matter was ironed out before the board and finally went to a magistrate in Hull. The Minister of Labour sent it there. I talked with some of the people who appeared before that magistrate, and they told me that the employer went in and stated his side of the case, that they came in and stated their side, and that the magistrate, trained to administer in respect of decisions in criminal law, sat to hear the case.
Industrial relations are human relations. There is no prosecution or defence of a criminal in a matter of this kind; rather there is a duty to deal with the technicalities of industry and the mechanics of unionism. The magistrate must have some knowledge of agreements, contracts and procedure. But the magistrate does not have that knowledge, and after sitting around for some time and spending a large sum of money the case is dropped. I am not speaking disparagingly about the magistrate in question, because he is all right in his own field.
