speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, today the house has heard a number of questions asked and a number of answers given; and there has been noticeable a certain measure of impatience in certain quarters that still further questions are being asked. On a number of occasions the minister has repeated that we have more complete information than similar elective bodies elsewhere, but the repetition of that statement does not make it correct. If anyone wants to know how correct or otherwise that statement is, it is only necessary to read any one of the great metropolitan dailies of the United States. One can then see the amount of information that is given in congress in regard to every detail of national defence, except that which comes under the real veil of secrecy such as the details of the development of the hydrogen bomb; the development of atomic energy, and even that is now subject to some limitations; the development of secret weapons that have not been announced. There is a discussion on those that are generally known, although they are still described by the use of the particular term "secret weapons".
Moreover, when we are told we have more information than is available at Westminster, that again is simply not so. At Westminster the estimates go before a subcommittee on estimates, and the members who make up that committee have the right to call and do call-within this last year they have, as on other occasions-upon senior staff officers of the different branches of the service. These men are questioned about the details connected with those military services. It was only in the late afternoon that some measure of information was given which had been sought all day. Over and over again an attempt had been made, not only today but earlier, to get some idea of the real breakdown of the figure that is given for the active army. We are told that there are in excess of 40,000 members of the active army. We are told of their high state of training. In so far as their training goes, with whatever limitations there are upon that training, it is true that they are keen; that they are devoting themselves to that training; and that they give an example on parade which might well be accepted anywhere as a standard of what military appearance should be. Only in t

Supply-National Defence late afternoon we learned that of those 40,000 the hitting force, and it is the hitting force that counts, is in the neighbourhood of 4,000 in the brigade group. We were given that information indirectly, because it was stated that the brigade group was about 80 per cent of strength, and we know the establishment of a brigade group. Therefore, subject to whatever additional figures may be added by the minister, the hitting force that we have available through our land army is something of the order of 4,000 men.
Having said that, it is appropriate to point out that the staff, the officer body, and the men generally of the active army are called upon to train the reserve army. Therefore the relationship of the staff, and of non-combatant to combatant, could not be expected to bear the same proportions as a group of military formations in the field. Nevertheless there must surely be some reason for concern, and there must be a recognition of the lack of balance, when out of some 40,000 our apparent hitting force is in the neighbourhood of 4,000. I say, Mr. Chairman, it is our apparent hitting force. It may be greater than that, and if it is we are still waiting to be told what the figures are. I hope we will not again in this chamber hear a statement that this information might help Russia. Surely we are talking in terms of reality, and not in terms of children's make-believe. We are talking in terms of the threat of a military power that has some 160 fully armed divisions in the field, and that has a potential of some 600 divisions that could be quickly brought into military service. It is that potential to which the free nations of the world are now directing their attention, and which they are seeking to restrain by their combined strength.
The only people who will be misled or the only people who will be in any way fooled by hiding information are the people of Canada who should know exactly what the facts are and who are prepared to meet those facts. The people of this country will respond to a challenge. The people of this country, if they are told of the need really to prepare ourselves for the test that lies ahead, will undoubtedly meet whatever reasonable demand is made upon them or any call for sacrifice. But it would be criminal folly for any Canadian to forget what happened in 1914 and in 1939, and not to remember what happens to the bravest men if they are confronted with superior armed force and a determined enemy who has been preparing for active aggression with the deliberate intention of using his weapons for that aggression.
In so far as the figures are available, we do not know. I hope that the minister will

indicate that the figures are much better than they now appear. But one of the things that this committee should know and should insist upon knowing-and this insistence should come from every part of the chamber -is how many of the active forces are in headquarters, how many are staff, how many are in command headquarters, how many are engaged in the work in the various military establishments across the country and in the armouries as well. We should know what the proportion is of each of those groups brought right down to the actual hitting force itself. When 1 speak of the hitting force, I am not including those vitally important services-and may I emphasize the words "vitally important services"- such as the medical service, the army service corps and the various organizations required to support troops in the field. Their place is as a component part of any successful military effort. But the effort from the staff organization down and up again is all related to What hitting force can be put in the field. If our hitting force is only of the order of
4,000	or 5,000 men, and if that is the total number of men that we could put into the field if the call came tomorrow, then there is a disproportion that should alarm everyone here and everyone in this country; because that proportion is not one that is in keeping with any balanced allocation of military tasks.
When the minister was asked about those forces, and it was mentioned that 80 per cent of the establishment of the brigade group would be in the neighbourhood of 4,000, he said quite properly that it must be remembered that behind and associated with that were the reserve units. There again is something about which we should have a great deal more information than we have now before we even think of passing this item. We must remember that this item is the one that embraces the whole broad field of military expenditure in the general field of military training.
The minister pointed out that certain units of the reserve forces which have been mentioned are in a high state of training and that they would be able in a short time to give an excellent account of themselves. He was asked, "Within what time?" His answer was, "Varying times". I do not think any words in this discussion have been more descriptive of the nature of the information that we have than the answer that was given to that question, "Within what time?" The answer was, "Varying times". What is meant by "varying times"?
Do not let anyone accept the statement that we are getting accurate information when

we are simply told that the reserve units could be put in the field in varying times. We know from experience that units of the reserve forces were put in the fields in varying times in the last war, and they ranged from two and a half years upwards. It takes a long time to bring a reserve unit up to combatant standards, unless its training has been on a combatant level, whether it has full equipment or not. I greatly question whether there is a single reserve unit in Canada today that, with any justice to the men in that unit, could be put in the field against a trained army in less than six months. We are talking in terms of what can be done in the face of an immediate threat, not what can be done at some distant time.
I would hope that the members of this committee would ask that the Minister of National Defence speak with words that have the same clarity as those used by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, because the Secretary of State for External Affairs left no doubt that I can see in reading the words as to his interpretation of what happened so recently in London when the twelve member nations of the Atlantic community met there and reached certain agreements. Speaking as the man who had actually been there, speaking on behalf of Canada, and speaking as the man who represented Canada, the Secretary of State for External Affairs told us here in this chamber last Monday that never again could nations wait behind the ramparts of sacrifice of other nations to build up their strength to defend themselves. Those are clear words and they are words that face the reality. Never again, he was telling us in effect, will there be that period which we were given in the first world war and in the second world war to make up for the time which had been lost in making any effective preparation to meet the threat of war which was actually before us. Never again can we hope for a channel to protect freedom in the way that the channel protected Britain as the great outpost of freedom in 1939 onwards until the free nations were ready to re-invade the European continent.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs also used words which were open to no doubt when he said that this agreement laid' down a new principle and that principle was-and he used an illustration to show what he meant -that each nation within this group of twelve nations would decide what task it could best perform and what things it could best produce as part of the combined effort. Let us take the illustration of the battleships, and this has already been mentioned; but in the face of the uncertainty of the statements that have been made, it obviously needs to be
Supply-National Defence repeated. He pointed out that if the battleships could best be built by one nation, then other nations would not build them; but he pointed out that such an economy of forces- and may I emphasize the words "economy of forces"-would only be possible if the other nations knew that the nation which was building the battleships would put them to immediate use in the event that a threat had to be faced; and that applied to aircraft, to armoured vehicles and to everything else. It is not only that the nation which can best produce those things will produce them and train with them, but that whole principle rests upon the clear understanding that if other nations leave that job to a nation that can best perform it, that nation which is doing that particular task will carry out that task at the moment that the task is of importance.
We have no such definite statement from the Minister of National Defence. On the contrary, we are told that what has happened in London calls for no change that should be announced to us now. All over this country the agreement was hailed as one of the historic documents of our time. The newspapers very naturally, in editorials and in feature articles, spoke of the fact that this presented the possibility of a reorganization of our forces which could increase the effectiveness of those forces and at the same time make it possible to economize in some of these things. And yet we are told that there is no change from what has been placed before us for so long, and that this calls for no new announcement, no new plan, no statement that there will be a re-adjustment of the proportion of units or anything of that kind.

speechtext: What suggestion have you to make about a re-apportionment of units?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I will make that suggestion in a moment. In so far as these details are concerned, I asked last night-and I asked in the hope that the minister would comply with the request-that the minister agree to prepare a statement which could be presented to this house and could be printed as an appendix to the records of the house, which would show the actual military formations in this country, would show the headquarters organization here in Ottawa, would show the command organizations, would show the groups within those various commands; would show the number of infantry units, the number of artillery units, the number of engineering units, signal units, medical units and all the other units required by a land force; would tell us the number of air units of different kinds, whether of fighter, bomber or other squadrons, would give us the numbers and types of ships, both in

Supply-National Defence active service and included in these estimates for construction or for the beginning of construction during the current year.
The minister comes forward with nothing of that kind. He still talks in generalities, still talks in very vague and uncertain terms of the things that must be secret, and we do not even know what he thinks should be secret and what should not. There is no mystery about the organization of our forces in this country. We have a headquarters staff here in Ottawa, and we should know- and I propose, to ask in detail-exactly the number of staff officers in this headquarters, what the military staff organization is under them, what the general civilian body is that is employed here in Ottawa; what the number is at command headquarters, what the number is at every other military location throughout Canada, and the number of people, not giving them in individual points, but the number employed at armouries and at other establishments for maintenance and otherwise. These figures could be given without producing volumes to do that task.
Let us look at the situation. We have this headquarters here. The general staff is situated here, and all the supporting organization. Then we have in this country five commands. We have these commands divided as follows: We have the eastern command, with headquarters at Halifax; we have the Quebec command with headquarters at Montreal; we have the central command with headquarters at Oakville; we have the prairie command with headquarters at Winnipeg, and the western command with headquarters at Edmonton. In turn these commands have certain special duties and certain special tasks. One of the things that should be explained to us, when the detailed organization of these commands is given to us, is what is being done at these commands for divisional organization, and what is the divisional organization within these commands; because that also is something that relates to the type of training that we are giving, and whether there should be a reallocation of forces in this country.
Also there is the question of the interchangeability of units between eastern and western commands because of the similarity of their tasks. Certainly it is not in any of these secret categories when we recognize the fact, which is not stated in any of these records, but nevertheless is fully recognized and generally known but has to be stated in order to examine the whole picture, that our military establishment is based upon the acceptance of the proposition that we will have six divisions, four independent infantry brigades, two independent tank brigades as well as certain ancillary troops.
[Mr. Drew. 1

The divisions in the various commands are as follows. The eastern command has the fifth infantry division; the Quebec command has the third and fourth infantry divisions; the central command has the first infantry division and the second armoured division; the western command has the sixth armoured division and the Pacific command has part of the fifth infantry division, so that the fifth infantry division is made up of the parts that are in both the eastern and western commands.
When the Minister of National Defence asks what should be considered, well, here is something that certainly should be considered, namely, whether or not the decisions that were made in London so short a time ago have any bearing on whether there should be a greater concentration of armoured divisions than of ordinary infantry divisions. I think the minister should tell us whether he thinks that with the developments of the past few months, let alone a few years, infantry divisions can ever possibly be expected to go into active service except in association with armoured divisions; and whether the whole plan should not be to create fighting teams in which the armour and infantry are integrated at all times without any degree of separation between the two formations.
The war establishment, and it is the active service establishment that we are contemplating in this discussion of an armoured division, consists of an infantry brigade of four infantry battalions, an armoured brigade, four armoured regiments, divisional troops. These divisional troops include divisional artillery, self-propelled regiments, self-propelled antitank regiments, armoured car regiment, motor battalion division, signal regiment, divisional engineers, divisional service corps, divisional medical corps, divisional ordnance corps, divisional electrical and mechanical engineers. That is the type of force that is included in one armoured division on a war establishment. I think that is the kind of thing we should be asking at a time like this, when the very survival of this nation rests upon the subject we are discussing.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: What do you want to tell the world about it for?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext:
As I was saying, when the very survival of this nation depends upon the subject we are discussing. First: what is the actual situation in regard to each one of those units that are embraced in an armoured division of this kind? As would be indicated by the very fact that the fifth infantry division is divided between the east and west coasts, it is clear that the fifth infantry division is for coast defence in both coastal areas.

Then, outside of those particular troops that have this particular task there are five other divisions and in addition four independent infantry brigades and two independent tank brigades. These are all reserve organizations. I am convinced that there is no one who would speak with any measure of responsibility who would suggest that with the most concentrated training that could possibly be conceived those units could go into action in less than six months-and many of them would require a great deal more than that.
It is in the light of that situation that we must then go back to the words of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who said that we have come to the time now when never again can preparation go forward behind the ramparts of sacrifices of some other nation, but that the task now is to have a hitting force that can be put into the field the moment the demand comes.
When the Minister of National Defence asks what can be done, then I say to him that what can be done and what should be done-and we should be having staff officers right here to tell us-is, in the light of this new principle enunciated last Monday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, to tell us what is the maximum hitting force which can go into action immediately and that we as a nation can maintain.
That is the question. And on the answer to that question depends the answer to the demand for money which is being made in this House of Commons. It may be a great deal more than the money that is asked for, and it may be less. It may be that, if our forces are organized on a highly efficient basis, with every unit trained to work as a team that can go into action the moment the whistle blows, we actually would save millions and scores of millions of dollars. On the other hand, if on the advice of the staff, and with that advice presented to members of parliament, it is clear that more money is needed, then I am satisfied that parliament and the people of Canada will vote whatever money is needed to preserve that freedom which means more than life itself to our people.
But let us know what is the force. I say the definition is simple, and the definition is not contained in anything that has been put before us here. The definition is simple, and it is this:	We are members of the Atlantic
community of nations. According to the Secretary of State for External Affairs we have agreed to become part of a team of free nations pooling all their strength for the preservation of their freedom. We have agreed
Supply-National Defence as a free nation to pool that strength upon a basis which will economize by using that strength which each nation can best produce.
Our contribution may well be limited in the field of a land force; it may be very great in the air. I have no doubt that that is our major role. It certainly would be very great in hard-hitting armoured units. Also there are undoubtedly certain types of service craft which this country has learned to make so well, manned by men who have shown as high a natural instinct for seamanship as the members of any navy in the world. There again our task is to determine what proportion of those should be used, and whether in the light of this new principle enunciated by the Secretary of State for External Affairs we are to maintain aircraft, carriers, cruisers, destroyers, submarines or vessels of any other kind.
All we are asking, and I am sure what the people of Canada are asking, is to know what the facts are and to know the best contribution we can make and, knowing that, then to relate the expenditure of money called for by parliament to the most effective organization of a force of that kind that can be put into operation the very moment danger of war should threaten. It is upon that basis that we will have not war but peace.
If there is one clear and tragic lesson that has emerged from all the dreadful and heartbreaking evidence at Nuremberg last year, it is the clear evidence that where there were two world wars there could have been peace, if the free nations of the world, with all their vast resources, and that greater energy which freedom gives, had only had the vision to stand together and to say to Germany and to other aggressors before war actually came, "We will give everything we have to save this freedom that we love so much. Do not be misled into believing that we have gone soft, or that we are not prepared to fight for the freedom which you threaten."
Today there is only one possible enemy in the world-only one. Never before in the whole history of the world have the lines been drawn so clearly. Those of us of my age and over have lived through the most eventful years in the whole history of the world. My memory as a small boy goes back to the days immediately following the South African war, and to the time when those who served in that distant field came back. To us they were almost like men from Mars. They had been in a distant world the rest of us could not understand. They had come from a distant land the rest of us would never know. There was romance, there was glamour-yes, there was an appeal about the 'thought of marching men on the distant veldt that had

Supply-National Defence no relationship to the tragic hardships, the disease, the death and the horrors that went with that struggle in a comparatively limited part of the world.	-
Then, in the years between 1901 and 1914, there were a number of great powers any one of which might have threatened the peace of the world. There was Germany, the Austrian empire of 55 million people, France, Italy, China, Japan, Great Britain and the United States. They were all strong powers.
Then war came, and out of the holocaust of war a very limited number of nations carried on as great powers. Actually in the years after the war Japan in the east and Germany in Europe presented the only real threat. Mussolini could not build a formidable army although he put many men under arms. Two threats were there and we knew they were threats. Russia was not yet a threat in the same way because it was still gathering its forces together under the new tyranny which had emerged. But it would be a good thing for us to recall that the real driving power that created the tyrannies in Germany and Italy was communism itself. It was because of the rise of communism in Germany after world war I, after the dreadful horrors of the communist governments of Prussia, of Saxony, of Bavaria and other German states, it was after the horrors of communism in Italy as well, that these dictators emerged and built up their military power.
In the Orient the military power of Japan was built up upon another basis. But there was that threat; we saw it and we knew it. War came. The war destroyed much. But for Great Britain, for the commonwealth, for the United States, for many nations in Europe and the rest of the world, thank God, it did not destroy freedom. But freedom has been lost in many parts of the world. Freedom is being lost day by day, under the threat from one power and one power alone.
That power has vast military strength which was built up largely by the assistance given by Great Britain, by the United States and by Canada as well. Let us be under no delusion as to the strength of Russia in many lines. I am not questioning the wisdom of the decisions arrived at at the time, but we sent some of the finest electrical equipment ever produced in Canada to help rebuild the great power plants on the Don, the Dnieper, and the Dniester. Those great projects are producing the power for the munition plants of Russia where they are turning out arms and equipment with the help of the conscripted skill of eastern Germany which they control.


It is not an easy picture to accept. We know that the machine tools which they cannot turn out as yet on a satisfactory basis were supplied by ourselves in limited quantities, by the United States, by Great Britain, by Sweden and other countries which are able to make machine tools of the highest quality.
That threat is there and must be dealt with, not by promises of what can be done within six months, within a .year or within two years; it can be blocked only if we face the realities of what it means. We, along with other nations, must create armed forces in being, not armed forces on paper, not armed forces that can go into action in six months or a year.
The Minister of National Defence knows that I had some experience with this problem and it is because of that experience that I am concerned about any delay in the reorganization of our forces in keeping with the principle that has been laid down. As he has stated, I had the privilege of being 'the president of the Canadian Artillery Association at a time when all the defence associations came together for the purpose of drafting a plan for the reorganization of our land forces. At that time there was a complete disproportion between the infantry units, the artillery units and the other units. The resolution upon which the reorganization took place was a simple one calling for the integrated organization of the land forces in Canada on the basis of not less than four and not more than six divisions on an active service basis. With the acceptance of that principle the six-division basis was adopted and the reorganization took place. It took several years and it was only because there were several years in which to carry out that reorganization that it was possible for the reserve units of this country to be mobilized as they were in 1939.
We are confronted now with another demand for a type of armed force that will be adapted to the principle enunciated so clearly last Monday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. We want to know exactly what is the maximum hitting force that can be put into the field right away, not something that will take months to prepare but right away. Whatever that force is, we want to see the equipment and we want to see the training. We want to see the sort of organizations which can put those units in the field at the earliest possible moment. So much for the land force.
What is our role in the air? That too must have been dis,cussed. There cannot be any secrecy about this. As the organization of

our air force is developed it is known to everyone. They know what the types are. The Russians do not think that a Vampire or other jet machines are bombers. They do not think they are anything else but what they are. They can tell by the type of machine just what it is intended for. When we have five jet squadrons, which is the present objective, they will know that those five jet squadrons are for a particular purpose. If we have jet transport squadrons or turboprop squadrons or squadrons of any other kind, they will know what they are for. For that reason, let us know what is needed. Let us know what fits into this pattern. Then let us insist that the plan be completed.
The same is true of the naval force. Let us know whether the aircraft carrier is still part of the force or whether it should be reallocated to the navy of Great Britain. On the other hand, let us know whether we should have more aircraft carriers. Let us know what the task is.
In this respect may I point out that it is not enough for us to be told by the minister what he thinks this is; we should have the evidence of what is required. It is for this house to say how far it is prepared to go and to insist that this government, with the full support of the members of parliament, must create the most efficient fighting unit consistent with this new principle which will economize our effort and which will make it possible to develop our strength within this team of free nations.
Beyond the armed forces is the question of military supply. We have the statement of General Howard, chairman of that board, that the developments are not as advanced as they should be. We should know how much of this money is needed by that board under the chairmanship of General Howard. Having regard to the allocation of tasks, we want to know that that also is brought up to date.
That is the broad picture. We are not dealing simply with marching men; we are not dealing simply with aircraft flying over our heads; we are not dealing simply with the magnificent sight of ships; we are dealing with the last chance for freedom in our generation. That is what it is. It is time that every one of us grasped this problem with full recognition of all that it means. If there is one call that should come to us from those whose memory is perpetuated in the cemeteries, money for which is a part of the requirements to be voted, it is: Do not again put young men against steel, iron and explosives without the steel, iron and explosives that they need for their task. Do
Supply-National Defence not pit flesh and blood against steel. Do not test the bravery of a free people beyond endurance. We have risked that twice. Let us not try it again. That is the issue before us. In the light of that issue I once again urge the Minister of National Defence to give us the complete breakdown to which we are entitled.

Not necessarily, but I say that the problem of our national defence is a problem which must be decided by parliament and the country, and one which must be decided in the light of the circumstances as they exist at the time. Hon. members will appreciate that I have made a good many speeches throughout the country about the communist menace. They will appreciate I have made a good many speeches to arouse interest in the work of our armed forces and

Supply-National Defence explaining their needs, but I do not feel it is necessary to make that kind of speech tonight.
I feel that this is one kind of audience which might have been spared the speech made by the leader of the opposition. He has made it before, and we agree with a great deal of it.
We are concerned now with voting $425 million for purposes of national defence for the year 1950-51. That is the matter before the committee. I must say I have been ready to take part in that discussion since the 17th of March when this department was the first to be brought into supply. We have not been assisted to any great degree in making any progress by the various measures that have been brought forward by opposition groups from time to time. But here we are. We have had two days of the most ample and general discussion. A .good deal of it has been first-class and very welcome; but why the leader of the opposition, the hon. member for Kamloops and other members of the opposition should in some way find fault with us because we have not anticipated meetings that have not taken place, because we have not anticipated decisions that have not yet been made, because we have not declared history before it has been written,
I just do not understand.
That has gone on for two days, apparently in some kind of notion that in the statements of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and myself there is room for finding some point of difference. I should like once and for all to scotch that type of childish effort to provoke some kind of division in the government. The Secretary of State for External Affairs and I have known each other for over twenty-five years. We have worked together on international conference after international conference. When he was away in London at the recent conference it was given to me to represent him in the house as Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs, as it has been my duty in his absence ever since he was appointed Secretary of State for External Affairs. So far as I know, when I have acted with him as his junior on a delegation, or when we have worked together on any other occasion, we have worked together as one person speaking the same language, as members of this government work together under the leadership of the Prime Minister. We have gone over the text of what the Secretary of State for External Affairs said and I think I have quoted parts of it twice, but I only did so because members of the opposition failed to quote the parts that were necessary to complete the picture. The statement is there. If you look at the statements made in consequence of the first meeting of the council of


ministers under the North Atlantic pact in Washington; then the defence committee held in Washington; then the defence committee held in Paris; then subsequently the defence committee held in The Hague; and finally the council of ministers held in London; you will see a record of gradual, steady but rapid accomplishment of the ends for which the North Atlantic treaty was signed by this and the other eleven nations.
Let no member of this house and no person in Canada ever fail to remember that among the nations which put forward the idea of this treaty, Canada, through the statement of the Prime Minister at the United Nations, was one of the first. That was followed through in our work in the working group. In fact I believe we were the first country to sign the pact, and then we were among the first to ratify it without a dissenting voice in either this house or the Senate. Make no mistake about it, any effort by anyone anywhere to indicate that we are less than faithful to our signature and desirous of the interests of freedom is an effort to distort the established record and to thwart the interests of the Canadian people.
Why should it be necessary for me to say this after we have gone through all these debates, and the discussion in the house yesterday and today? Only because an effort has been made to indicate that Canada, in some way or other, is doing less than she should. Sir, I am one who has had to face the Canadian people in some elections, and I never want to face any section of [DOT] the Canadian people unless I can say that we have done everything that is necessary to live up to our bond, to seek our interests, and to do what the Canadian people want. The record of the armed forces of Canada in the great war of 1914-18, and the second world war, has given us a place second to none among the nations of the world, irrespective of size. We have earned their respect, and we are going to hold their respect.
Why have the members of the official opposition brought up this series of questions as to whether we are going to make changes; whether we are doing enough; whether we should not suddenly stop in the middle of our defence preparations this year and make some other preparations, because of the declaration of an important principle? I do not know why they have done it. I do not see where they are getting. I do not see any political advantage from it. I certainly see no national advantage to it. I see nothing in the speech of the leader of the opposition that would help us in either raising forces for our own defence or meeting the enemy should he come tomorrow. I do not see it. I have been

trying through three years to develop the sort of idea that I believe is thoroughly understood by this country, and that is that defence is a matter of major government policy, of major national policy, because of the attitude of the Soviet union. Owing to that fact, we have been seeking increasingly large amounts from parliament in order to secure the means of defending ourselves, but also to contribute to the defence of other nations who think with us that we must defend our freedom where-ever it can best be defended. Towards that end I believe a good many hon. members on both sides of the house have spent their efforts. I believe also that, to a greater degree than ever before in the peacetime history of this country, the needs of national defence are recognized and appreciated by the people in every part of Canada, and no one has done more to arouse that appreciation and that recognition than the Prime Minister.
But far more than the efforts of any person have been the realities of the situation. On that account, as I say, we are seeking an increasingly large amount from parliament for national defence. This year we have come before you for $425 million. I shall not say for a moment that with $425 million we can guarantee Canada, or any part of it, against attack. I shall not say that with $425 million we can replace all the deficiencies that may be found in western Europe; that is ridiculous. What we must do is see what part of our national income, of our national budget, of our national production, we can spend on defence, having regard to our appreciation of the international situation. Then having regard to that sum, but always having arrived at it with regard to the international situation, we must see how we can best spend it. During this discussion I have not heard very much criticism of the work of the members of the Royal Canadian Navy, or the army, or the air force, and they are people who are our defenders today.
It is possible, of course, to say that we should spend a little more in respect of the air force; a little more in respect of the navy; a little more in respect of the army, or the reserve, or the active forces, or cadets. But every cent more that is spent in one direction must be taken from somewhere else. You cannot use these dollars that are voted by parliament more than once. You can use them for personnel, for construction or for equipment. You can use them for the navy, army, or air force. You can use them for active or reserve forces, but you cannot use them right across the board. The point which I believe must be emphasized before this committee is that, on the information I
Supply-National Defence have given today and having regard to comparisons that are available to us of the accomplishments of our navy and air force, and then from what we know of the army, the division seems to be as good as we can work out. I have not heard any suggestion that there is anything wrong with it. I have only heard suggestions that I should announce some change in consequence of some decision that has not yet been made. But I think that this committee will agree with my suggestion and also the people of Canada, judging from what I have seen of them-and I dare say I have travelled about the country on my job more than most other hon. members, meeting the people and trying to persuade them that what the defence forces need is their support and then explaining defence policy to the defence forces. What I have found everywhere is that the need is for appreciation, and that the defence forces are not only accepted but are respected to a degree that has never been attained before in our country's peacetime history.
Every now and then there is thrown out the suggestion that everything is fine with the defence forces but everything is wrong with the minister. I do not claim a bit of credit for anything that is good about the defence forces, and I think they are good; but I demand the right here or anywhere else to defend them, and I have done so from one end of the country to the other whenever the need has been apparent.
I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, to have taken up so much of the time of the committee, but I do not think I have taken up nearly as much as have some of the hon. members of the opposition who have made statements today. I should like to deal again with a matter I dealt with before; and always on these questions it is difficult to know how much one can go beyond the terms of the actual communique that we agreed to have announced. One of the things the leader of the opposition said was, "Let us know what is needed" and he said he was sure that the Canadian people would respond. I am finding that the Canadian people are responding quite well to the appeals that are made to them. But "Let us know what is needed", he said; and I ask, "Let us know what is needed, where, when, by whom, and with what?"
,1 would tell the leader of the opposition this, and here I think I have the precedent of General Bradley in the speech he made on April 14 to which I referred. The list of the requirements of the countries of the North Atlantic treaty far exceed their present

Supply-National Defence available resources of personnel or equipment. That is so in almost every computation of military needs. I do not suggest for a second that we should not take the list of requirements as being serious. Of course they are. But when he says, "Let us know what is needed", I say that we can only answer that in terms of what we think we should contribute to the common pool of defence, and then also relate that to our own local defence needs; and relate for our own local defence just as small a portion as is possible for us to relate in that way. We want to have in Canada engaged in static defence as small a force as is regarded as being needed. But then we get into the question of equipment, personnel and what is needed for balanced forces; and that is one of the questions which are coming before the deputies who have not met yet-they have not been appointed yet- and before the other agencies of the North Atlantic treaty organization.
I must say that I am astonished at being accused steadily throughout the last few days of not disclosing something that has not been revealed or yet disclosed to me or to anyone else in the world yet. I am also surprised at being accused of saying that we are not taking care of the future, not thinking ahead and so on, when all of our defence planning, as far as I can see and as disclosed to hon. members, has been based on the principle of continuing examination to meet changing circumstances. Just because we seem to have done so well in anticipation as not to require any change in the immediate future does not mean that we will not require a change over the long term or over the intermediate term. As I said today, we shall be ready and glad to discuss with our partners in the North Atlantic treaty ways and means of pooling our resources so that we can make the best possible use of them. But that does not remove from us in Canada the responsibility of trying to work out what is the best pattern for our forces. I must say that during the last few days or in the previous defence debates I have not heard anything which has caused us to alter greatly the pattern that has been worked out since the war. I must also say that we have heard a good deal, particularly from the hon. member for Nanaimo, which has confirmed us in the course that we have been following; and I hope that we shall hear more in the future to the same effect. But let no one try to separate us one from another by any charge based on false premises. And let no one suggest for a second that this government or this department is not doing everything in its power to press forward the preparation of our defences within the means put at our


disposal. In that I am sure we shall have the support of members from every part of the committee.

To come back to the remarks which the minister was making, he said that an effort had been made to show that Canada is doing less than she should. No such effort as that was made, Mr. Chairman. Nobody on this side of the house made any attempt of such a nature. What we have done is to have asked for information. And it is information which we think we are entitled to get. There is surely nothing in the matter of asking for information which should cause the Minister of National Defence to say that an effort was being made to show that Canada is doing less than she should. Nobody has suggested that; nobody has thought it.
Then the minister asked this question: Why have the opposition been asking these questions? Well, by that he meant the questions that we have asked about the possible change in defence planning, and so forth, because of the agreements made last month in London. The answer to that is very simple. We have been asking the questions because we want to know the answers. What other reason is there for asking certain questions? The minister was making a great point of it. We asked these questions naturally because we want to know, and we think it is o-ur duty to know, what our defence policy is; whether there have been any changes in it as a result of these agreements which were made last month, and also how the defence policy is to be or is being implemented or carried out. That is why we have been asking these questions. There is nothing else we can do except ask them.
One reason that we have to ask them probably more often than we would like to ask them is that we do not get direct, straight answers to the questions. We have to keep

Supply-National Defence asking and asking over and over again to get anything like the information that we want. In other words, we draw it out in bits and pieces. If we could get a complete and full answer the first time, then we would not have to repeat the question, and ask for another bit of information on something else.
Finally the minister said he had not heard any criticism of the navy, the army or the air force. Certainly he has not heard any criticism of them. Why should he hear any criticism of them from us? They are carrying out the duties assigned to them, and the policy which is adopted by this government. So far as we have been able to determine, they are carrying them out very well. But what we are criticizing, what we are asking questions about, is the policy. What is the policy? That is what we are trying to find out, particularly as to whether these forces have the strengths, the equipment and so forth to be able to carry out these policies properly or not. That is what we are asking for, and that is what we want. In many cases these are not the answers we have been getting.

You don't need to talk, buttercup. Silence, as I said before, is golden. I am going to say very little more. Maybe

some of my friends to my left will listen to
me when I say this: The heart of government is in Britain; the muscle of government is in the United States; the brains of government are in Canada today.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Well now, Mr. Chairman, let us all be perfectly clear about one thing, and that is that there is no one in this chamber who has been casting any reflections on Canadians in any of the armed forces-

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext:
-and anyone who suggests that any member of this house did cast such a reflection is not worthy to sit in the House of Commons. Because I might point out that interest in the men of our armed forces is not the exclusive privilege of the hon. member for Mackenzie, or any other member in the House of Commons. There are members in the house who have as much reason for interest in and concern about those in the armed forces as any others who have spoken. I am prepared to attribute that interest to every member. I hope we will keep the discussion on the basis of the broad problem, and not try to divert the discussion to any such improper suggestions as those which were made.
When we are asked why any question should be raised-

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: On a question of privilege.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Sit down.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Did not the leader of the opposition say that there was not a force in Canada today that was trained well enough to meet the enemy?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, that merely indicates how necessary it is that things be repeated frequently, because if the hon. member had listenedi, or if he had been capable of remembering, he would have remembered that what was pointed out was that we were told that there was a brigade group with an approximate number of 4,000 men who would be in position to go into active service right away. When the minister was asked how soon these other reserve units could go into action, if necessary, his reply was simply that it could be done at some uncertain time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Various times.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext:
At some varying times. "Varying times" is the very expression I used, and "varying times" is something that not one of us can define. Varying time is something that all of us should try to understand. I, for one, have tried to impress upon the minister the desirability of preparing a statement which

would show a break-down. 1 do not believe for one moment that the minister is not fully aware of the kind of statement that would answer the request that has been made, and would greatly simplify this discussion.
I have stopped to point out that during the lifetime of many of us here we have seen events move through to the point where there are only two camps and where, if we succeed in our effort, we have brighter hopes of peace than ever before and, if we fail, there is nothing but disaster.
In so far as what we are discussing is concerned, I have merely suggested that we discuss it with a recognition of the seriousness of the problem. I am urging the minister to prepare such a statement. If he will not do it, then there is no alternative but to take these items one by one, go through them and get the information that could easily have been presented in a statement. That would have saved time-and the other way will take a very long time.
Now I shall ask my first question.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Filibuster.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext:
"Filibuster"-no; it is a subject about which we not only have the right but the duty to know something. That information could have been given to us in the form of facts, and perhaps disposed of in a very short time. However, since we have not got that I shall proceed to ask my questions.
My first question is this: How many officers, N.C.O.'s and other ranks are employed at headquarters at Ottawa?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Carried.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: No, it is not carried.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: I believe the answer to that question was given before. However, I am checking up.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Then, I shall put the next one: How many civilians are employed at headquarters in Ottawa?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: I think that was answered, too.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Silly question No. 2.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I do not think that was answered. I have a note down here in connection with it.
Mr.' Drew: If it has been answered, then it would be very easy to give the information to me. We want it right up to date. I should like to ask that I be given answers to both the first and second questions.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext:

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: How many civilian personnel were involved or employed in departmental administration in 1949-50, this year, and in the year 1948-49?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Perhaps it would simplify things if the minister would explain why there is an increase of something in the neighbourhood of $1,175,409 in the general administration item?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: I can give the hon. member the answer to that. It is almost entirely due to increased inspection services. A total Of $758,433 of the increase is due to increased inspection services made necessary by increased purchases of defence equipment.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Where was that shown last year?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Under the same item.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: How many extra personnel are performing the increased services?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: In the inspection branch?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Eighty-nine people. In addition there is an increase in the amount of work let out by contract by the inspection services.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I am trying to be helpful and not critical, but in every other department you find a separate item for general administration while in the Department of National Defence everything is lumped in the one huge general item. It would be much easier if we could discuss under general administration the problems which we discuss under that item in other departments.
I noticed that other departments list under that general administration item the number of officials employed which I assume covers the administration of the several branches at Ottawa. But in the case of the Department of National Defence no such breakdown is given to us. Would it be asking too much to ask the minister to tell us what the ministers of other departments tell us, the number of officials employed in the various branches of the department and how much of this general administration item is for pay and allowances of officers and other ranks and personnel at national defence headquarters and in the several commands and divisions throughout the country? It is impossible from this one general statement to get any idea of what is covered by general administration in this particular department.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: I wonder if the minister would like to put the list of temporaries on the record rather than read them? He has had a hard day and it may save time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: I have enjoyed this day.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I was only trying to save the time of the committee. In the long list that


the minister has just read, did that include officers of the army, navy or air force, or are they all civilians?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: All civilians.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is this amount of $3,466,205 all paid out to civilians?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Oh, no, the total for salaries that I mentioned was $2,202,728. Those are civilian salaries and wages as shown on page 168 of the details.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Are any military personnel included in those?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Not at all.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Then it is all paid to civilians?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is the point I asked a moment ago. Then in addition to the $3,466,000, which is for departmental administration, there are a certain number of officers of all three services employed at headquarters in Ottawa.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Can you give me any idea what the pay and allowances of the total number of officers and other ranks employed at national defence headquarters would amount to?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: That figure changes from day to day, as the hon. member must appreciate. I can get the figure for him as of any date he mentions. It will take a little time but that can be obtained.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: The minister has just given us a list of the permanent civil employees at headquarters under the item of departmental administration. Therefore he must be able to give us the actual number of both permanent and temporary employees. He said 760 temporaries, but how many permanent?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: There are 115 permanents and 760 temporaries.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Those figures just include national defence headquarters?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Not for any of the
commands?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext:
That includes national
defence headquarters for the three services?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: This is departmental administration in respect of the whole department but not within each service.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: You referred to the inspection service. Is it carried out entirely by civilians?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: No. We have attached to the inspection service a number of service personnel in order to secure the advantage of service experience and training, and also the reverse with regard to inspection. It is mostly civilian but at headquarters in Ottawa there are a limited number of rather senior service personnel.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Are their pay and allowances included in the amount you quoted for the inspection service?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: No, they are additional. They are paid out of the pay and allowances of the armed forces. As I understand it, they are attached, not seconded.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: That would not include of course any inspection services dealing with the efficiency of personnel or the state of training of the various units?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: They are purely an inspection service dealing with the inspection of equipment, buildings and that sort of thing.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Does that include buildings which are under departmental-

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Perhaps they may have to do with some of the materials that go into the buildings that are constructed by the department itself, but that would be a very minor item. They have to do with equipment and supplies.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Do they inspect buildings which are being erected now for the department?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: In the various headquarters?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext:
No. A very large part of the construction of defence quarters, particularly married quarters, is done by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and we do no part of the inspection of that. I would have to verify to see whether or not our inspection services have to do with the inspection of materials or work entering into such part of our construction program as we do ourselves. My impression would be that they do not but I can verify that. They have to do with the inspection of armament, equipment, motor vehicles, clothing and the like. As an offhand figure, I would suggest that
Supply-National Defence they inspect certainly in excess of 50,000 or
60,000	contracts a year representing approximately $150 million.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is that in addition to any inspection staff employed with the Canadian Commercial Corporation?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: No, the Canadian Commercial Corporation is a procurement agency for the Department of National Defence. We are the consumer and we provide the inspection services.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: You provide the inspection services in that case?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: And that also applies to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: No, not to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. We do not provide any inspection service.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am sorry for that because certain complaints have been made regarding the type of houses which have been constructed. I believe you had a communication only a short time ago from the city of Victoria making a complaint. We accept these houses without any inspection? There is no check at all by the department?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: The houses are not delivered to the Department of National Defence. In effect they are leased to members of the defence forces. It is quite true that it is not precisely the same as a civilian lease because they do not receive their allowances. In their place they receive a house. In effect the defence personnel occupying Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation houses are in the position of tenants. Of course we try to see that the houses are in good shape before they are delivered. We do everything possible towards that end but we are not responsible for the condition of the houses.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext: Do personnel have to live in them?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext:
There has been no difficulty about forcing personnel to live in the houses. There is a waiting list at every military establishment for such houses.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday we will take up the second reading of Bill No. 268, an act to amend the Foreign

Business of the House Insurance Companies Act, 1932; second reading of Bill No. 269, an act to amend the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, 1932. I understand these two bills will be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce.
Where are they now?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
They received first reading by leave of the house just before six o'clock. We will then take up the resolution in the name of the Minister of
Trade and Commerce concerning the Defence Supplies Act; Bill No. 89, an act to provide for the publication of statutory regulations. Then we will move to go into committee of supply and call one item of the Department of National Revenue, that item to stand. We will then take up the estimates of the Department of Agriculture.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Monday. June 12. 1950
